shortReport.title: Day 2
shortReport.description:
Preparing the PowerPoint presentation of the projects, 
Teams will present their presentations
Other teams will evaluate the presentations and give feedback

comments.text: In this collaborative exercise, intern teams will develop, deliver, and critically assess project-based PowerPoint presentations. The process is divided into three key phases: preparation, presentation, and peer evaluation.   1. Team Preparation of PowerPoint Presentations Each team will create a clear, concise, and visually supportive PowerPoint presentation that effectively communicates the objectives, methodology, findings, and conclusions of their project. Teams are expected to: Structure content logically: Include a title slide, agenda, problem statement, methods, key results/discussion, conclusions, and next steps or recommendations. Design for clarity: Use bullet points, visuals (charts, diagrams, images), and minimal text per slide to reinforce spoken explanations—not replace them. Coordinate roles: Assign team members to present specific sections, ensuring smooth transitions and cohesive delivery. Time management: Adhere to the designated time limit (e.g., 10–15 minutes) to allow for Q&A and feedback.   2. Team Presentation Delivery Each team will present their slides to the class or evaluation panel. During the presentation, the presenting team should: - Speak clearly and engage the audience. - Avoid simply reading slides; instead, elaborate on key points. - Manage timing and transitions professionally. - Respond to questions thoughtfully during a brief Q&A session following the presentation.   3. Peer Evaluation & Feedback While teams present, all other teams act as active evaluators. Their role is to observe critically and provide constructive feedback. Each evaluating team will complete a structured evaluation form (digital or paper) addressing criteria such as: Content quality: Depth, accuracy, relevance, and logical flow. Slide design: Readability, visual appeal, effective use of graphics, and minimal text overload. Delivery: Clarity, pace, eye contact, teamwork, and time management. Q&A performance: Ability to answer questions clearly and confidently.  After all presentations, or immediately following each one (as directed), evaluating teams will share written or verbal feedback. Feedback must be: Specific (e.g., “The diagram on slide 5 clarified the process well” rather than “Good job”). Constructive (e.g., “Consider reducing text on slide 3 and using a graph instead”). Respectful and professional, focusing on the work, not the individuals.   Goals of the Process For presenting teams: Gain experience in public speaking, visual communication, and handling questions under real-time observation. For evaluating teams: Develop critical thinking, active listening, and the ability to articulate constructive feedback—key skills in collaborative work environments.   Outcome All teams will receive a compilation of peer feedback along with the instructor's evaluation. This multi-source input helps identify strengths and areas for improvement, fostering a learning environment grounded in mutual respect and continuous growth.

Day 6 is focused on bridging user-facing design with disciplined backend coding practices. Interns will begin by translating their project requirements into tangible front-end layouts, then shift focus to mastering Test-Driven Development (TDD) – a professional methodology that prioritizes writing tests before implementation code.   Morning Session (9:00 AM – 10:45 AM): Front-End Design Development  Interns will work on developing the front-end design of their assigned projects. This session emphasizes creating intuitive, responsive, and visually coherent user interfaces based on previously defined project specifications.  Key activities include:  - Translating wireframes or mockups into functional front-end code (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, or the framework specified for the project) - Ensuring layout consistency, navigation clarity, and basic interactivity - Applying principles of user experience (UX) such as logical information hierarchy and visual feedback - Preparing to integrate the front end with backend logic in subsequent days  Deliverable by end of this session: A working draft of the core front-end interface for each project.     Tea Break (10:45 AM – 11:00 AM)  A 15-minute break for interns to refresh before transitioning into the backend-focused TDD module.     Late Morning Session (11:00 AM – 12:30 PM): Introduction to Test-Driven Development (TDD)  This hands-on session introduces the Test-Driven Development (TDD) philosophy – a professional software development practice where tests are written before the actual code. Interns will learn by doing, starting with a simple product function before applying TDD to a Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm.  Part 1: TDD Philosophy & Practice (11:00 AM – 11:45 AM)  - Concept introduction: Explain the Red-Green-Refactor cycle:   - Red – Write a failing test for a desired feature   - Green – Write the minimal code to pass the test   - Refactor – Improve the code while keeping tests green - Guided practice: Interns implement a simple product function (e.g., `multiply(a, b)`) using TDD, writing tests first, then the function, then refactoring.  Part 2: Applying TDD to Depth-First Search (DFS) (11:45 AM – 12:30 PM)  Building on the TDD rhythm, interns will apply TDD principles to implement a Depth-First Search algorithm on a graph or tree structure.  Steps:  1. Write a failing test for a specific DFS behavior (e.g., visiting nodes in correct order, finding a target value) 2. Implement just enough DFS code to pass the test 3. Refactor for clarity and efficiency 4. Repeat for edge cases (empty graph, missing node, cyclic graphs)  Learning outcomes:  - Understand how TDD leads to cleaner, more testable, and more reliable code - Gain confidence in writing tests before implementation - Apply systematic testing to recursive algorithms like DFS     Wrap-Up (12:30 PM)  Brief recap of the day's accomplishments: completed front-end drafts, hands-on TDD practice, and a tested DFS implementation. Instructors will provide pointers for further practice before the next session.    Overall Goal for Day 6:   By the end of the day, interns will have made tangible progress on their project's user interface and adopted a professional testing discipline (TDD) that they can apply to all future coding tasks, starting with graph algorithms like DFS.

shortReport.title: Day 4 Report
shortReport.description: Continue practicing TDD principles with the Depth-First Search algorithm; group collaboration on edge cases for unit tests (09:00--10:30)

comments.text: Session Overview  This session deepens interns' mastery of Test-Driven Development (TDD) by continuing hands-on work with the Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm. Following individual practice, interns will transition into group collaboration to systematically identify, write, and test edge cases – a critical skill for building robust, production-ready software.   Part 1: Continued TDD Practice with DFS (09:00 – 09:45)  Building on prior introductory work, interns will further develop their DFS implementation using the Red-Green-Refactor cycle.  Activities:  - Expand the DFS algorithm to handle additional requirements, such as:   - Returning the order of visited nodes   - Searching for a specific target value   - Handling different graph representations (adjacency list vs. matrix) - Write new tests first for each desired behavior, then implement just enough code to pass - Refactor existing DFS code for improved efficiency, readability, and recursion safety (e.g., avoiding stack overflow on deep graphs)  Key TDD principles reinforced:  - Never write new functionality without a failing test first - Keep the cycle short (seconds to a few minutes per iteration) - Trust the tests – refactor fearlessly when tests are green   Part 2: Group Collaboration on Edge Cases for Unit Tests (09:45 – 10:30)  Interns will form small teams (3–4 members) to systematically explore and test edge cases for DFS. This collaborative approach surfaces scenarios that individuals might overlook and mirrors real-world code review practices.  Collaboration process:  1. Brainstorm edge cases for DFS on graphs/trees, such as:    - Empty graph (no nodes)    - Single node graph    - Disconnected graphs (components with no paths between them)    - Cyclic graphs (preventing infinite loops)    - Very deep graphs (testing recursion limits)    - Graphs with duplicate values or self-loops    - Null or invalid inputs  2. Write unit tests collaboratively for each edge case (still following TDD principles).    - One intern writes a failing test, teammates review it for correctness and clarity    - Another intern implements the minimal code to pass the test    - The group refactors together, discussing trade-offs  3. Run the full test suite and analyze results.    - Identify gaps in test coverage    - Discuss why certain edge cases break naive DFS implementations    - Document lessons learned about defensive programming   Learning Outcomes  By the end of this session, interns will be able to:  - Confidently apply TDD to recursive algorithms like DFS - Identify, prioritize, and test edge cases that typical implementations miss - Collaborate effectively on unit test design and code implementation - Appreciate how group testing improves code reliability and catches bugs early   Deliverable  Each group will produce: - A completed DFS implementation with a comprehensive suite of unit tests covering standard cases and edge cases - A brief written summary (2–3 bullet points) of the most surprising or instructive edge case encountered

name: C.A.T.I.A. Travel FBBA
plan:
Overview of the Operation of a Travel Agency
The operation of a travel agency functions as a dynamic intermediary between travel suppliers (airlines, hotels, tour operators, cruise lines, insurance providers) and end consumers (leisure travelers, corporate clients). Its core mission is to simplify the travel planning process, provide expert guidance, and deliver seamless, memorable travel experiences.

The operational workflow typically follows five key stages:

1. Customer Inquiry & Needs Assessment
The process begins with direct interaction through walk-in clients, phone calls, email, or website chatbots. Agents conduct a structured needs analysis, identifying the client’s budget, destination preferences, travel dates, group size, special requirements (e.g., accessibility, dietary needs), and purpose of travel (leisure, business, honeymoon, group tour).

2. Product Sourcing & Itinerary Design
Using a combination of Global Distribution Systems (GDS – e.g., Amadeus, Sabre), preferred supplier contracts, and dynamic packaging tools, the agency searches for available inventory. Agents assemble a customized itinerary, selecting from:

Transportation (flights, trains, car rentals, transfers)

Accommodation (hotels, resorts, vacation rentals)

Ancillary services (tours, travel insurance, visa assistance, event tickets)

3. Quotation, Booking & Ticketing
A detailed quotation is prepared, clearly stating the total cost, inclusions/exclusions, cancellation policies, and payment schedule. Upon client approval and deposit, the agency secures reservations by issuing electronic tickets, vouchers, and booking confirmations. Payment collection may involve credit card processing, bank transfers, or installment plans, with the agency earning revenue through commissions (from suppliers) and service fees (from clients).

4. Pre-Departure & Documentation Management
Prior to departure, the agency provides a travel pack including:

E-tickets and accommodation vouchers

Visa and passport requirements

Travel insurance policy documents

Local customs, health advisories (e.g., vaccinations), and emergency contact numbers

Final itinerary and check-in instructions

Proactive agents also conduct a pre-travel confirmation call or email to verify all arrangements.

5. In-Trip Support & Post-Travel Follow-Up
The agency maintains 24/7 emergency contact availability to handle real-time disruptions (flight delays, hotel overbookings, medical issues). After the client returns, the agency follows up for feedback, resolves any disputes with suppliers, processes post-travel claims (e.g., baggage loss), and nurtures the relationship for repeat business through loyalty programs or newsletters.

Key Operational Assets:

Technology Stack: CRM (customer relationship management), GDS, online booking engine, accounting software

Licensing & Bonds: IATA/IATAN accreditation, seller of travel registration, consumer protection bond (depending on jurisdiction)

Supplier Network: Negotiated commission structures, allotment contracts, and preferred partnerships

name: Chemical Engineering
plan:
Химическая технология – 3-й курс (10-дневная стажировка): Геохимическая аналитическая лаборатория

• День 1: Введение, обзор лаборатории, картирование процессов и обращение с материалами
– Прибытие, оформление документов.
– Знакомство с руководителем стажировки и наставниками. Ознакомительная экскурсия по лаборатории.
– Вводный инструктаж по лабораторной безопасности, СИЗ (акцент на обращении с кислотами, вдыхании пыли и высокотемпературных рисках), а также по внутренним правилам. Изучение паспортов безопасности химических веществ (MSDS) с фокусом на протоколы хранения химикатов и утилизации опасных отходов.
– Анализ планировки лаборатории не просто как набора рабочих мест, а как технологической блок-схемы (process flow diagram).
– Введение в лабораторную информационную систему (LIMS) и отслеживание образцов горных пород от приёмки до конечного результата.
• День 2: Механическая обработка и материальный баланс
– Изучение механического измельчения образцов пород (при наличии); фокус на распределении частиц по размерам и его влиянии на площадь поверхности и последующую кинетику растворения.
– Задание: рассчитать материальный баланс по линии пробоподготовки с учётом возможных потерь из-за пылеобразования и налипания материала на оборудование.
– Документирование использования гравиметрического анализа как технологической операции разделения (например, определение влажности/потери при прокаливании).
• День 3: Реакционная техника кислотного вскрытия и выщелачивания
– Анализ кислотного вскрытия как периодического реакторного процесса. Изучение влияния концентрации реагента, температуры и перемешивания на скорость растворения минеральных матриц.
– Задание: определить стехиометрию реакции вскрытия для целевого минерала и рассчитать необходимый избыток кислоты для обеспечения полной конверсии.
• День 4: Термодинамика растворов
– Изучение поведения ионов металлов в концентрированных кислотах; обзор коэффициентов активности и пределов растворимости.
– Задание: оценить риск осаждения в жидких пробах перед инструментальным анализом и предложить стратегии его предотвращения (например, использование комплексообразующих агентов).
• Дни 5–7: Инструментальный анализ
– Практическое изучение атомно-абсорбционной спектроскопии (AAS) и дуговой искровой оптико-эмиссионной спектроскопии (OES).
– Задание: проанализировать пределы обнаружения и градуировочные графики для конкретных элементов (например, микроэлементы/следы металлов).
– Введение в масс-спектрометрию с индуктивно связанной плазмой (ICP-MS) для многоэлементного анализа.
– Задание: сравнить чувствительность различных инструментальных методов, используемых в лаборатории.
– Протоколы контроля качества (QC): изучение использования холостых проб, добавленных стандартов (spikes) и дубликатов для валидации результатов анализа.
– Сравнение лабораторных данных с внутренними стандартами и определение соответствия результатов требуемым технологическим допускам.
• День 8: Плавка – высокотемпературный процесс
– Изучение процесса плавки как жидкостной экстракции и пирометаллургического разделения.
– Осмотр печей для плавки/пробирного анализа. Фокус на теплопередаче и теплоизоляции.
– Задание (тепловая энергия): оценить тепловой КПД печи на основе соотношения подведённой энергии и энергии, необходимой для плавления/сплавления.
• Дни 9–10: Итоговый отчёт
– Завершение отчёта по стажировке с акцентом на применение принципов химической технологии (тепло- и массообмен, кинетика, термодинамика) к аналитическому процессу. Также сравнение лабораторных операций с крупномасштабными промышленными процессами химической технологии применительно к извлечению критически важного сырья (металлов) из руд.

shortReport.title: 2 day Internship of Chemical group
shortReport.description:
The students arrived at the internship site at 9:00 a.m., with a 100% attendance rate recorded. During the day, they were given the opportunity to become closely acquainted with the practical activities carried out in the laboratories. At the beginning of the session, Munira Numonovna Melikova – Lead Engineer for Occupational Health, Labor Protection and Safety at the Analytical Laboratory Complex provided an introductory briefing on occupational safety, laboratory safety regulations, and emergency response procedures.
Subsequently, under the supervision of Seyyare Sabriyevna Memetova, Head of the Chemical Spectral Laboratory, and accompanied by Lenara Serverovna Omerova, Chief Methodologist of the Chemical Spectral Laboratory, the students became familiar with the processes of gold and silver extraction from ores, methods of weighing ore samples and chemical reagents using analytical balances, as well as analytical techniques for determining sample composition through the use of chemical reagents.
In addition, the trainees visited the Atomic Emission Spectrometry Laboratory. Particular interest was generated by the processes involving the transition of atoms in the analyzed samples to high-energy states, atomic emission analysis, atomization of samples, and excitation of atoms in high-temperature ICP (Inductively Coupled Plasma) environments with temperatures ranging from approximately 6,000 to 10,000 K (about 5,700–9,700 °C). The students observed how chemical elements are identified through the spectral emissions produced by excited atoms within the plasma medium.
The students also observed the thermal treatment of soil and ore samples, including calcination in muffle furnaces and the separation of constituent components using various chemical reagents.
Furthermore, in the Chemical Spectral Laboratory, students A. Igamberdiyev, N. Namozova, D. Toxsonova, I. Ikramov, and Q. Talatzoda independently conducted a laboratory experiment to determine magnesium ions in water samples. During the experiment, specific reagents were added to the samples, resulting in the formation of a white precipitate of magnesium ammonium phosphate. The obtained results confirmed the presence of magnesium in the water samples and demonstrated the practical application of chemical analytical methods.
The experiment was based on the following reaction equation:
Mg²⁺ + NH₄⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → MgNH₄PO₄↓
The students also conducted a laboratory experiment to determine chloride ions in water samples. During the analysis, silver nitrate solution was added to the samples. The formation of a white silver chloride precipitate confirmed the presence of chloride ions in the investigated water samples. This experiment demonstrated one of the classical qualitative methods used in chemical analysis of aqueous solutions.
The reaction proceeded according to the following equation:
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl↓
In addition, the students observed a laboratory experiment for the determination of calcium ions in water samples. During the experiment, ammonium oxalate solution was added to the samples, resulting in the formation of a white calcium oxalate precipitate. The obtained results confirmed the presence of calcium ions in the water. This method is considered one of the classical approaches for determining the mineral composition of water.
The experiment was based on the following reaction equation:
Ca²⁺ + C₂O₄²⁻ → CaC₂O₄↓
During this internship, the students were provided with an opportunity to connect their theoretical knowledge in chemical engineering with real industrial and laboratory processes. They became familiar with geological and technological sample preparation methods, techniques for the identification and extraction of precious metals from ores, chemical and spectroscopic analytical methods, the operation of analytical balances, and procedures for determining magnesium, calcium, and chloride ions in water samples.
Special attention was given to occupational health and safety requirements and laboratory safety regulations. The internship contributed to the development of practical skills in working with laboratory equipment and modern analytical instruments, enhanced students’ ability to interpret chemical analysis results, and broadened their understanding of technological processes employed in industrial enterprises.
The knowledge and practical experience gained during the internship contribute to strengthening the professional competencies required for future careers as qualified chemical engineers.
Among the expected outcomes of the internship are the development of students’ abilities to apply chemical analysis methods in practice, work independently in laboratory and industrial environments, analyze technological processes, and formulate scientifically sound and technically justified conclusions based on obtained results.
It is expected that by the completion of the internship, students will have gained a deeper understanding of the operating principles of modern laboratory equipment and will be better prepared as specialists capable of effectively addressing real-world industrial challenges encountered in chemical and related industries.

•	Sandwich panels
•	Prepainted galvanized steel (in coils and sheets)
•	Roofing profiles and corrugated sheets
•	Stainless steel pipes
•	Metal structures of any complexity
Next, the students received occupational health and safety training. Following this, one of the company's leading specialists organized an engaging tour. Transportation across the plant's territory was provided via minibuses.
After lunch at the factory cafeteria, classes continued in a well-equipped classroom.
Upon completion of the program at 17:00, the group of students returned to the city by the university bus.

Taking into account the capabilities of Azia Metall Prof, it was decided to revise the industrial internship schedule.
The group is divided into two subgroups:
Subgroup 1: E. Lashchuk, A. Yuldashev, Sh. Marufova, D. Kuziboev, Sh. Dusiev, R. Negmatova.
Subgroup 2: S. Sobirov, S. Azimova, M. Kholikjonov, A. Negmatov, M. Soliev.
Internship Schedule (June 8 – July 3, 2026):
•	Week 1 (June 8–12): Subgroup 1 — at the plant; Subgroup 2 — remote. 
•	Week 2 (June 15–19): Subgroup 1 — remote; Subgroup 2 — at the plant. 
•	Week 3 (June 22–26): Subgroup 1 — at the plant; Subgroup 2 — remote. 
•	Week 4 (June 29 – July 3): Subgroup 1 — remote; Subgroup 2 — at the plant. 
The internship will conclude on July 3, 2026.
On June 8, 2026, the students were assigned to the departments of Accounting, Logistics, Marketing, and Information Technology.
Absent: E. Lashchuk, D. Kuziboev, R. Negmatova.

This morning, I discussed optimizing the internship program with the Head of HR. Specifically, we added an economist, who previously served as a deputy director at a large foreign corporation, to the company's team of internship supervisors. I also met with the CEO, Mr. Z.Y. Aminov, and briefed him on the progress of the internship. Students Sh. Marufova, Sh. Dusiev, and A. Yuldashev are actively participating in their practical training, applying their knowledge in a real-world setting. Specifically, within the logistics department, Sh. Dusiev familiarized himself with the following workflows: Data Management and Documentation: Organizing, verifying, and preparing document packages in compliance with corporate standards. Customs Clearance and Declaration: Mastering specialized software used by customs brokers to submit cargo declarations. International Logistics: Studying the rules and step-by-step procedures for completing international customs transit declarations. Overall, it was a highly productive day.

Report on Day 4 of the Industrial Internship for Students at the Metallurgical Plant
In the accounting department, interns thoroughly studied current cost accounting and fixed asset depreciation. Students mastered primary documentation entry and verified incoming invoices for raw material purchases.
In logistics, interns familiarized themselves with finished steel supply chains and route optimization. They directly participated in coordinating delivery schedules to transport manufactured goods.
In the specialized workshop, students mastered operational material accounting. They recorded metal production volumes, actual billet consumption, and monitored shift output logs.
In the information technology department, interns tested new modules of the plant ERP system. They verified material accounting databases and configured automatic report templates for management.
The fourth day successfully reinforced theoretical knowledge and showed the inner connection of all enterprise services.

Report on Day 5 of Students' Industrial Internship at the Metallurgical Plant
• In the accounting department, students continued studying the current document workflow. They mastered the reconciliation of accounts with coke and ore suppliers and examined the depreciation calculation procedures for the specialized workshop equipment.
• The interns analyzed the specifics of the plant's transport logistics. They studied the rules for drawing up waybills for raw material deliveries and familiarized themselves with the operations of the dispatch service.
• The information technology student successfully completed the next stage of designing the corporate web resource. An intuitive navigation panel was fully formed, and the content distribution logic was thoroughly developed. The created information architecture ensures quick user access to key sections, optimizes internal transitions, and lays a solid foundation for further user interface (UI) visual design.
• The fifth day of the internship allowed students to gain a detailed understanding of the core operations in related departments and to establish a framework for the upcoming week's tasks.

Report on Day 6 of Students' Industrial Internship at the Metallurgical Plant
* Accounting Department: Students focused on the preparation of the weekly financial summary and analyzed the structure of production costs. They studied the distribution of overhead costs across blast furnace workshops and participated in the preliminary verification of tax documentation.
* Logistics and Dispatch: The interns investigated the optimization of internal transport within the plant. They analyzed the timing of loading and unloading operations for finished metal products and learned how to handle deviations from the standard delivery schedule.
* Information Technology: The IT student initiated the visual design phase of the corporate web resource based on the previously approved architecture. They selected the corporate color scheme, created typography standards, and developed high-fidelity mockups for the homepage and key navigation elements.
* Summary: The sixth day enabled students to transition from studying isolated departmental operations to understanding integrated plant workflows, setting clear objectives for the consolidation of their practical findings.

Daily Internship Report:
During today's internship, the trainees thoroughly studied the process of configuring shared access to printers over a network (Shared Printer). They successfully installed the necessary drivers on the device and tested its correct operation. Additionally, they gained practical skills in identifying and resolving various technical issues that arise during printer connectivity.
The following tasks were completed during the work process:
* Network Configuration: studied printer settings, activated the Printer Sharing feature, and explored network connectivity options for other users.
* Driver Management: analyzed driver-related errors, installed compatible versions, and performed system updates.
* Troubleshooting: applied diagnostic methods to restore communication and verify network permissions in scenarios where the computer failed to detect the printer.
* This practical experience reinforced knowledge in network printer connectivity, user rights management, driver administration, and technical troubleshooting. The experience gained will serve as a solid foundation for configuring IT infrastructure in offices and enterprises in the future.

During today's intensive practical session, the trainees gained hands-on experience with core IT infrastructure, system administration, and cybersecurity tools. Through RDP, they mastered securing and managing remote computers and servers. Using Hyper-V hypervisor technology, they successfully practiced creating virtual machines, allocating resources, and configuring virtual networks.
The trainees thoroughly analyzed Windows Server 2022, the backbone of large enterprise networks, focusing on its specific features like Active Directory services. To handle critical system failures, they thoroughly studied the Sergei Strelec WinPE bootable environment, utilizing diagnostics, data recovery, and password reset tools. Concluding the session, tasks were assigned to apply these technologies in practice, strengthen cybersecurity, and enhance system administration.

Today, a hands-on experiment was conducted on managing a dual-boot system. Windows and Kali Linux were installed on the computer. During the session, boot issues related to Kali Linux were analyzed, and their resolution methods were thoroughly investigated. First, the GRUB (bootloader) error occurring at startup was examined. By verifying BIOS/UEFI settings, the Windows Boot Manager and Kali Linux boot entries were studied, and the exact mechanics of the boot order were successfully analyzed. Following this, the contents of the EFI partition were inspected to identify boot files belonging to Kali Linux, which were then safely removed. Using "Disk Management" and the DiskPart command-line utility, the overall disk structure was analyzed, existing partitions were examined, and the partitions dedicated to Kali Linux were successfully deleted. Additionally, the status of the Windows Recovery Environment (Windows RE) was verified, and its operational principles were studied. Practical knowledge was gained regarding unallocated disk space reclamation, the specific function of EFI partitions, the overall importance of recovery partitions, and the internal mechanisms of the Windows boot process. As a result, the computer was successfully transitioned from a dual-boot configuration to a Windows-only system, the GRUB error was completely resolved, and a significant amount of disk space was successfully reclaimed.

On June 18, 2026, during the professional internship at the metallurgical plant, extensive documentation processing was successfully carried out. This involved verifying and systematizing various corporate invoices to ensure total data consistency, accurate financial details, and strict compliance. As part of studying foreign economic activity, key accounting and declaration processes were thoroughly mastered. Special attention was paid to complex import and export operations involving metal products, such as coils, sandwich panels, and profiles. Additionally, comprehensive hands-on familiarization was completed with modern digital solutions. These included the E-Contract system, the Didox.uz electronic document management platform, and the Cargo Customs software used for cargo clearance. Ultimately, the work performed provided a deep, practical understanding of the enterprise's entire foreign economic activity structure.

Internship Report: Day 11 (June 19, 2026)

* Operations in Didox.uz: Generated, verified, and sent electronic invoices (e-invoices) and certificates of completion to counterparties.

Day 12: Study of Factory Economic Planning and the Pyramid of Pain Concept
The twelfth day of work placement focused on analyzing the enterprise's planning and economic activities alongside studying modern cybersecurity methods.
During the meeting with the factory economist, the budgeting processes for revenues, expenses, procurement, and payments were examined in detail. Special attention was given to analyzing profit and loss statements, comparing current indicators with previous plans, and identifying causes of financial deviations to improve organizational efficiency.
The second part of the day covered the "Summit" topic in IT security. The Pyramid of Pain concept was thoroughly analyzed, along with a simulation of attacker activity. The IT session explored network artifacts, IP addresses, domains, file hashes, and TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures). It was established that blocking TTP layers protects infrastructure much more effectively than merely restricting basic indicators. This session successfully strengthened skills in threat detection and defense strategy development.

Internship Report — Day 13
Content of Completed Activities:
The thirteenth day of the internship was devoted to administrative and accounting activities within the organizational structure of the metallurgical plant. The main block of tasks involved professional documentation management: a thorough audit of incoming invoices for compliance with corporate standards, as well as their subsequent sorting and preparation for archiving. To optimize office workflows, the redistribution and systematization of physical records were carried out, significantly improving the efficiency of information retrieval.
Special attention was paid to the activities of the Accounting Department. Under the supervisor's guidance, the accounting process for salary advances for the plant personnel for the month of June was executed. This task involved calculating the number of employees who received an advance (over 300 individuals) and entering the relevant data into the enterprise's information system. This procedure is essential for the correct generation of payroll sheets and the subsequent deduction of these amounts from the total wages. The practice allowed for the consolidation of skills in using specialized software and the study of interaction algorithms between the financial department and the production workforce.

Report on Day 14 of the Industrial Internship for Students at the Metallurgical Plant
In the accounting department, interns reconciled quarterly financial statements and analyzed financial performance metrics from the internship period. Students generated final depreciation schedules and fully closed current accounts for raw material procurement.
In the logistics department, trainees evaluated the overall efficiency of implemented routes and analyzed logistics costs in detail. They prepared a final summary report on optimizing transport flows for finished steel over the two-week period.
In the specialized workshop, students finalized material accounting outcomes and conducted an inventory of remaining billets. They compared planned metal production targets against the actual results of completed shifts.
In the IT department, interns finished final testing of the new ERP system modules and resolved identified bugs. They configured automated dashboards to visualize analytics for corporate management.
The fourteenth day successfully consolidated integrated management skills and demonstrated the students' readiness for independent professional practice.

Internship Report: Day 15
On the final day of the internship at the metallurgical plant, students focused on comprehensive evaluation and program closure. In the accounting department, trainees compiled the final financial dossier and archived reconciled quarterly statements. The logistics department concluded operations by presenting the transport flow optimization report to senior management and archiving performance metrics. In the specialized workshop, interns conducted a final safety audit of the production lines and documented the verified billet inventory data. Meanwhile, the IT department handed over the fully tested ERP modules and initiated user training sessions for the plant's administrative staff. The afternoon was dedicated to an inter-departmental presentation where students summarized their two-week findings. This concluding day successfully validated the practical competencies acquired, marking the official completion of the industrial internship program.

On the sixteenth day of the industrial internship, students shifted focus toward post-program feedback and documentation refinement. The logistics department analyzed the initial executive feedback on their transport optimization report to draft secondary efficiency adjustments. Meanwhile, the IT department gathered initial performance metrics from the newly deployed ERP modules and resolved minor administrative user queries. The afternoon concluded with an official feedback session where plant supervisors evaluated student performance. This additional day reinforced operational continuity and finalized all remaining administrative handovers.

The final day of the industrial internship focused on data consolidation and the formal handover of responsibilities. Meanwhile, the IT department archived ERP performance metrics and revoked temporary system access credentials. Post-Internship Evaluation and Career Alignment
The day following the official conclusion of the program focused on personal performance evaluation and academic integration. In coordination with academic advisors, interns began structuring the comprehensive technical report required for university credit registration.

name: Digital Economy 3 year
plan:
Module 1: Immersion, Analytics, and Data Visualization (Days 1-8)
•	Day 1: Arrival, Orientation, and Digital Culture.
o	Arrival at the company. Paperwork.
o	Meeting with the HR manager and the assigned mentor.
o	Orientation session: company structure, key departments, data security and confidentiality policies.
o	Observing the digital culture: how internal systems are used, how communication takes place.
o	Assignment (Before the internship): Discuss your learning plan with the mentor.
•	Day 2: Analytics Department (BI) - Tools and Data.
o	Rotation: Business Intelligence / Analytics Department.
o	Introduction to the company's BI tools (Power BI, Tableau, Looker, etc.).
o	Overview of data sources: where the company gets data from (CRM, web analytics, social media, transactions).
o	Assignment: Create a diagram of the company's main data sources.
•	Day 3: Data Processing in Excel.
o	Assignment (Analytics): Receive a dataset from the mentor (e.g., sales data or user behavior data). Perform cleaning, filtering, and sorting. Add calculated columns.
•	Day 4: Data Visualization in Power BI / Excel.
o	Assignment (Visualization): Based on the processed data, create a dashboard in Power BI (or Excel). Include: sales trend chart, top products, geographical distribution (if data is available).
•	Day 5: Data Interpretation and Conclusions.
o	Analyzing the created dashboard.
o	Assignment (Reporting): Write a brief analytical report (1-2 pages) with key conclusions and recommendations based on the visualized data. Present the report to the mentor.
•	Day 6: CRM and Customer Experience.
o	Rotation: CRM / Customer Experience Department.
o	Studying the CRM system. How customer data is collected, how the audience is segmented.
o	Assignment: Analyze one customer segment and propose a way to improve engagement with it.
•	Day 7: Basics of Statistics for Business.
o	Applying statistical methods to business data.
o	Assignment: Calculate the correlation between two indicators (e.g., between advertising spend and sales). Draw a conclusion about the presence/absence of a relationship.
•	Day 8: Weekly Report and Feedback.
o	Preparing and submitting the first weekly progress report.
o	Meeting with the mentor to discuss the results of the first week.
o	Day off/Self-study: Systematizing the module's materials.
Module 2: AI, Innovation, and Digital Marketing (Days 9-16)
•	Day 9: Introduction to AI for Business.
o	Rotation: Data Science / AI or IT Department.
o	Overview lecture from a specialist: how AI is applied in the company (chatbots, forecasting, personalization).
o	Assignment: Record three business problems that the company solves using AI.
•	Day 10: AI Tools - Workshop.
o	Demonstration of working with AI tools (e.g., for time series forecasting or natural language processing).
o	Assignment: Under the mentor's guidance, try using a simple AI tool (e.g., Google Colab with a pre-trained model) for forecasting on training data.
•	Day 11: Digital Marketing and E-commerce.
o	Rotation: Digital Marketing / E-Commerce Department.
o	Studying the company's digital marketing channels (SEO, contextual advertising, social media, email marketing).
o	Analyzing the e-commerce sales funnel.
o	Assignment: Analyze the effectiveness of one of the advertising channels (if data is available) using metrics like CTR, CPC, conversion rate.
•	Day 12: User Behavior Analysis on Website/App.
o	Working with web analytics systems (Google Analytics, Yandex.Metrica, or similar).
o	Assignment: Compile a report on key traffic metrics for the last month: number of visitors, bounce rate, pages per session, traffic sources.
•	Day 13: Innovation and Business Models.
o	Rotation: Innovation / Business Development Department.
o	Studying innovative business models in the company's industry (subscription, freemium, marketplace, etc.).
o	Assignment: Conduct an analysis of the company's own business model using the Business Model Canvas – fill out 3-4 blocks.
•	Day 14: Industry Best Practices.
o	Researching competitors and market leaders.
o	Assignment (Benchmarking): Compare one of the company's processes/products with a similar one from a leading competitor. Identify gaps and propose ideas for improvement.
•	Day 15: Digital Transformation - Strategies.
o	Discussing the company's digital transformation strategy with the mentor.
o	Assignment: Document one example of process automation in the company (which process was automated, what technologies were used, what effect was achieved).
•	Day 16: Weekly Report and Feedback.
o	Preparing and submitting the second weekly report.
o	Meeting with the mentor to discuss the results of the second week.
o	Day off/Self-study: Systematizing materials on AI, marketing, and innovation.
Module 3: Startup Planning, Fintech, and Finance (Days 17-24)
•	Day 17: Developing a Business Idea.
o	Rotation: Innovation Department or independent work with the mentor.
o	Brainstorming: generating ideas for a new product/service/startup within or outside the company's current business.
o	Assignment: Formulate one business idea and describe its value proposition.
•	Day 18: Market Research and Customer Validation.
o	Developing hypotheses about the target audience and their needs.
o	Assignment: Create a questionnaire (Google Form) for potential customers to validate the idea. Identify channels for collecting responses.
•	Day 19: Feasibility Analysis.
o	Assessing the technical, operational, and financial feasibility of the idea.
o	Assignment: Fill out a feasibility analysis table for your idea (resources, technologies, estimated costs, potential risks).
•	Day 20: Fintech Operations and Digital Payments.
o	Rotation: Finance Department / Fintech Department.
o	Studying the payment systems used by the company (integration with banks, e-wallets, acquiring).
o	Assignment: Draw a diagram of the payment flow from the customer to the crediting of funds to the company's account.
•	Day 21: Basics of Financial Accounting.
o	Introduction to key financial concepts: revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses, net profit, cash flow.
o	Assignment: For your business idea, create a simplified P&L (Profit and Loss) forecast for the first year.
•	Day 22: Budgeting and Forecasting.
o	Studying the budgeting process in the company.
o	Assignment: Assist the finance department in collecting and reconciling actual data for one budget line item for the past month.
•	Day 23: KPIs and Metrics.
o	Studying key metrics for digital startups (CAC, LTV, Churn rate, MAU/DAU).
o	Assignment: Calculate one of the metrics for a hypothetical or real company product based on available data.
•	Day 24: Weekly Report and Feedback.
o	Preparing and submitting the third weekly report.
o	Meeting with the mentor to discuss progress on the startup idea and financial aspects.
o	Day off/Self-study: Refining the startup idea's business plan.
Module 4: Integration, Reporting, and Project Defense (Days 25-30)
•	Day 25: Preparing a Comprehensive Business Plan.
o	Consolidating all work on the startup idea into a single document: value proposition, market analysis, financial model, action plan.
o	Consulting with the mentor on structure and content.
•	Day 26: Preparing a Pitch Presentation.
o	Creating a presentation for investors or management (10 slides) based on the business plan.
o	Practicing the pitch structure: problem, solution, market, business model, team, finances.
•	Day 27: Preparing the Final Internship Report.
o	Writing a draft of the final report, including all sections: data analytics, AI applications, innovation, fintech, startup project.
o	Including all created dashboards, reports, diagrams, and analytical findings.
•	Day 28: Final Review and Rehearsal.
o	Finalizing the report and presentation based on the mentor's comments.
o	Rehearsing the oral defense (pitch) in front of the mentor or colleagues.
•	Day 29: Submitting the Report and Preparing for Defense.
o	Finalizing the diary and final report.
o	Receiving the completed supervisor evaluation form.
o	Final consultations.
•	Day 30: Final Presentation and Internship Completion.
o	Presenting the internship results and the startup project to the mentor, department heads, and possibly company management.
o	Demonstrating analytical skills, understanding of AI and innovation, and entrepreneurial competencies.
o	Discussing the experience gained, its connection to the curriculum, and future plans.

shortReport.title: Day 1: Arrival, Orientation, and Introduction
shortReport.description:
Day 1: Arrival, Orientation, and Introduction

Today, seven third-year students majoring in Digital Economy started their internship at Kapitalbank.

At 9:00 a.m., we met with the bank’s HR manager Mrs. Firuza Farkhadovna. During the orientation session, she explained how the bank operates, introduced the basics of banking, and discussed the importance of confidentiality and information security.

The students were introduced to the bank, its departments, and its staff members. In addition, the working hours, dress code, workplace rules, and the main responsibilities of the interns were explained.

At the end of the first day, the students gained a general understanding of the bank’s activities and the organization of work within the company.

shortReport.title: Day 2: Analytics Department (BI) - Tools and Data.
shortReport.description:
Host Institution: "Kapitalbank" (two branches) | Date: 02.06.2026
​Departmental Progress:
​Accounting: Students studied the structure of the Chart of Accounts for banks in the Republic of Uzbekistan. They observed the opening of the operational day in the Core Banking System (CBS) and learned how the branch's daily balance sheet is generated.
​Post-Control Department: Students were briefed on the bank's internal regulations and the Central Bank of Uzbekistan's requirements. Using archived documents, they studied methods for detecting operational errors and sorted cash vouchers.
​Credit Department: Students familiarized themselves with Kapitalbank's retail and commercial loan products. They examined the structure of a credit file and the checklist of documents required to assess a borrower's creditworthiness.
​Summary of the Day:
Students successfully integrated into their respective departments across two bank branches, transitioning from general orientation to working with regulatory frameworks and documentation. Attendance and discipline were fully maintained; mentors noted high student engagement. Today's objectives have been fully met.

shortReport.title: Day 3: Data Processing in Excel.
shortReport.description:
Day Objectives and Tasks
​To develop interns' skills in working with complex datasets and primary data exports from core banking systems.
​To train interns in methods of minimizing operational risks through proper data cleaning and verification.
​To master calculation automation tools aimed at optimizing routine tasks within specialized departments.
Practical Tasks, Alignment with Bank Functions, and Results
​Accounting Department
​Practical Tasks & Alignment: Cleaning registries of duplicates, blank rows, and system errors. Sorting and filtering data based on specified parameters (accounts, dates, transaction types).
​Result: Interns mastered the algorithm for preparing datasets for reconciling debit/credit turnovers and generating daily balances.
​Post-Control Department
​Practical Tasks & Alignment: Applying filtering and logical conditions to identify anomalies, missing fields, and non-standard amounts in operational day data exports.
​Result: Developed skills in the express auditing of electronic registries to detect operational errors and violations of bank regulations.​

shortReport.title: Day 4: Data Visualization in Power BI / Excel.
shortReport.description:
Today's day was dedicated to a key stage of working with data — visualization and the creation of interactive dashboards. Based on the data that students cleaned and prepared in previous days, they were required to build a report in Power BI (or Excel) to present business results.

Most of the interns successfully completed the task, demonstrating not only their technical skills in working with BI tools but also their understanding of which metrics are important for the banking business.The students approached the task like true analysts. In the dashboards they created, the three required sections were clearly highlighted. They also conducted a mini-session on geodata normalization and configuring data categories in Power BI.

shortReport.title: Day 5: Data Interpretation and Conclusions.
shortReport.description:
Today marked the completion of the first week of the student internship at Kapitalbank. The final day was dedicated to business analysis and the defense of their results. Based on the dashboards created the previous day, the students prepared brief analytical reports (1–2 pages) containing specific conclusions and recommendations for the bank's management, and presented them to me as their mentor.
​All interns successfully defended their work. The day demonstrated that the students are capable of not just working with the software (Excel/Power BI), but also transforming dry numbers into valuable business insight.
Task Results (Analytical Reports)
​In their reports, the students demonstrated a high level of analytical thinking.

shortReport.title: Day 6: CRM and Customer Experience
shortReport.description:
The sixth day of the internship was dedicated to studying the customer relationship management (CRM) ecosystem and analyzing customer experience (CX). Despite being assigned to back-office departments (Accounting and Post-Control), this cross-functional day helped the students understand how their routine work with documents and ledger entries directly impacts the final service delivery and customer loyalty.

​All students successfully mastered the theoretical foundations of banking CRM systems and studied the mechanisms of primary data collection, as well as the audience segmentation principles utilized by Kapitalbank.

The interns familiarized themselves with how the bank's algorithms segment the customer base (by income level, mobile app usage frequency, age, and transactional activity).

shortReport.title: Day 7: Basics of Statistics for Business
shortReport.description:
The seventh day of the internship was dedicated to mastering basic statistical methods and applying them to real-world banking business data. For the students from Accounting and Post-Control, this day provided an opportunity to transition from merely recording financial and operational metrics to performing deep analysis, uncovering hidden patterns, and evaluating relationships between indicators. The students examined how the bank utilizes statistics for process forecasting and optimization:
​In Accounting: How time-series analysis and correlation help forecast cash shortages (cash flow gaps), tax payment volumes, and operational expense dynamics.
​In Post-Control: How statistical quality control (the sampling method) allows for evaluating the overall level of operational errors without the need to conduct a comprehensive 100% audit of all documents.
​The program for Day 7 was completed in full. The students successfully mastered a tool that will enable them to automate components of analytical reporting in their respective departments in the future.

shortReport.title: Day 9 Summary (Module 2: AI, Innovation, and Digital Marketing)
shortReport.description:
As part of Day 9 of the internship program, 6 students are undergoing practical training at Kapitalbank in the Accounting Department (final control unit).

The students were introduced to the basic principles of applying artificial intelligence in the banking sector. An overview lecture was delivered by a specialist, covering practical cases of AI usage in the bank, including automation of customer interactions (chatbots), financial forecasting, and elements of service personalization.

During the rotation, students observed how AI technologies can be integrated into accounting control processes and transaction analysis. Special attention was given to the role of AI in reducing errors and improving data processing efficiency.

At the end of the day, students were assigned a task to identify and record three key business problems that are solved using AI within the bank. The students demonstrated strong engagement and understanding of the material, actively participated in discussions, and asked relevant questions.

Overall, the day was productive, and the objectives were successfully achieved.

shortReport.title: Day 10: AI Tools - Workshop
shortReport.description:
The tenth day of the internship was dedicated to introducing students to modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools and their applications in analytical activities within the banking sector. During the session, a demonstration of AI tools for data forecasting and information processing was conducted, along with practical examples of using pre-trained models in Google Colab.
The students undertaking their internship at Kapitalbank within the Accounting Departments participated in the workshop and, under the guidance of their mentor, completed practical tasks using training datasets. Particular attention was given to data analysis automation, forecasting techniques, and the interpretation of model outputs.
As part of the final assessment, the interns demonstrated an understanding of the fundamental principles of applying AI technologies to financial data, as well as the ability to use ready-made forecasting tools and analyze prediction results. All students successfully completed the assigned tasks, showed strong interest in modern digital technologies, and demonstrated readiness to apply their newly acquired knowledge in a professional environment.

shortReport.title: Day 11: Digital Marketing and E-commerce
shortReport.description:
On Day 11, the student interns continued learning about digital marketing and online sales in the banking sector.
During the rotation, they studied the main promotion channels: SEO, contextual advertising, social media, and email marketing. Bank specialists explained how these tools help attract and retain customers.
The interns also learned how the sales funnel works — from attracting a client to completing a service and further interaction.
Students assigned to the accounting departments continued their tasks under the guidance of supervisors. At the end of the day, attendance and activity were monitored.
Overall, the student interns showed good engagement and a better understanding of how digital tools work in a bank.

shortReport.title: Day 12: User Behavior Analysis on Website/App.

On the thirteenth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments were introduced to innovation and modern business models used in the banking industry.

Overall, the day was useful and engaging, and the students showed good understanding of modern business approaches.

shortReport.title: Day 14: Industry Best Practices
shortReport.description:
On the fourteenth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments focused on studying industry best practices and analyzing competitors.
During the day, interns researched market leaders and reviewed how other banks and financial companies organize their processes and services. They learned how to identify strong sides of competitors and understand current market trends.

At the end of the day, the interns prepared short reports with their findings and recommendations.
Overall, the day was informative and practical, and the students showed good analytical thinking and involvement.

shortReport.title: Day 15: Digital Transformation – Strategies
shortReport.description:
On the fifteenth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments learned about the bank's digital transformation strategy.

During discussions with their mentors, the interns explored how digital technologies help improve business processes, increase efficiency, and enhance customer service. They gained a better understanding of the importance of innovation and automation in the modern banking industry.

As part of the assignment, the students documented one example of process automation within the bank. They described which process had been automated, what technologies were used, and what results had been achieved, such as reducing processing time, minimizing errors, or improving overall productivity.

shortReport.title: Day 16: Weekly Report and Feedback
shortReport.description:
On the sixteenth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments completed the second week of their practical training.

The interns prepared and submitted their third weekly reports, summarizing the tasks they had completed, the skills they had learned, and the experience they had gained during the week.

The students also met with their mentors to discuss their progress, receive feedback, and identify areas for further improvement. The mentors answered questions and gave recommendations for the remaining weeks of the internship.

The rest of the day was dedicated to self-study. The interns reviewed and organized materials related to artificial intelligence, digital marketing, innovation, and business development to strengthen their understanding of the topics covered during the internship.

shortReport.title: Day 17: Developing a Business Idea
shortReport.description:
On the seventeenth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments focused on developing innovative business ideas.

During the session, the interns participated in brainstorming activities with their mentors and discussed different ideas for new banking products and digital services. They learned how innovation can create value for customers and improve business performance.

As part of the assignment, each student developed one business idea and described its value proposition by explaining the customer problem, the proposed solution, and the expected benefits.

Overall, the day encouraged creativity, critical thinking, and a better understanding of innovation in the banking industry.

shortReport.title: Day 18: Market Research and Customer Validation
shortReport.description:
On the eighteenth day of the internship, students learned the importance of market research and customer validation before launching a new product or service.

The interns discussed how to identify target customers, understand their needs, and test business ideas through surveys and feedback.

As part of the assignment, the students created a questionnaire using Google Forms to collect opinions from potential customers. They also identified suitable channels for distributing the survey and collecting responses.

Overall, the day helped students understand how customer feedback supports successful business decisions. Тhe day was useful for reflection, feedback, and preparation for the next stage of the internship.

shortReport.title: Day 19: Feasibility Analysis
shortReport.description:
On the nineteenth day of the internship, students focused on evaluating the feasibility of their business ideas.

During the session, they learned how to assess technical, operational, and financial factors before implementing a new project. The mentors explained the importance of identifying the required resources, estimated costs, available technologies, expected business outcomes, and possible risks. The students also discussed how proper planning helps organizations reduce uncertainty, improve decision-making, and allocate resources more effectively.

As part of the assignment, the interns completed a feasibility analysis table for their business idea. They described the human and technical resources required, estimated implementation costs, identified possible operational and financial risks, and suggested practical solutions to reduce these risks. The students then presented their findings to their mentors and received constructive feedback on their analyses.

Overall, the day strengthened the students' analytical skills, improved their understanding of business planning, and helped them develop a more structured approach to evaluating new business opportunities before implementation.

shortReport.title: Day 20: Fintech Operations and Digital Payments
shortReport.description:
On the twentieth day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments learned about fintech operations and modern digital payment systems.

During the rotation, the interns explored how payment transactions are processed, including bank integrations, acquiring services, and electronic payment solutions. They also learned how secure and efficient payment systems support daily banking operations.

As part of the assignment, the students created a payment flow diagram showing the movement of funds from the customer to the company's bank account.

Overall, the day provided valuable knowledge about digital finance and payment technologies used in the banking sector.

shortReport.title: Day 21: Basics of Financial Accounting
shortReport.description:
On the twenty-first day of the internship, students were introduced to the basic principles of financial accounting.

The interns studied key financial concepts such as revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses, net profit, and cash flow. They discussed how these indicators are used to evaluate business performance.

As part of the assignment, the students prepared a simplified Profit and Loss (P&L) forecast for the first year of their business idea.
Overall, the day improved the students' understanding of financial planning and business performance analysis.

shortReport.title: Day 24: Weekly Report and Feedback
shortReport.description:
On the twenty-fourth day of the internship, students completed the third week of their practical training at Kapitalbank.

The interns prepared and submitted their weekly reports, summarizing the work completed during the week, including business idea development, financial planning, and market analysis.

The students met with their mentors to discuss their startup ideas, financial assumptions, and overall progress. The mentors provided constructive feedback and recommendations for improving the business plans before the final project presentation.

The rest of the day was dedicated to self-study, during which the interns refined their business plans and reviewed the knowledge gained throughout the internship.

Overall, the day provided an opportunity to reflect on progress and prepare for the final stage of the internship.

shortReport.title: Day 30: Final Presentation and Internship Completion
shortReport.description:
On the thirtieth and final day of the internship, students working at Kapitalbank in the accounting and final control departments successfully completed their practical training. The interns presented the results of their internship and their startup projects to their mentors, department heads, and other representatives of the bank.

During the presentations, the students demonstrated the knowledge and skills they had developed throughout the internship. They explained their business ideas, feasibility analyses, financial forecasts, and market research, while also showing their understanding of artificial intelligence, digital transformation, innovation, and entrepreneurship in the banking sector.

The mentors evaluated the students' analytical thinking, communication skills, problem-solving abilities, and professional growth. They provided constructive feedback, discussed the strengths of each project, and suggested areas for future development.

At the end of the day, the interns reflected on the experience they had gained during the internship and discussed how the practical training supported the knowledge acquired through their university curriculum. They also shared their future academic and career plans and expressed appreciation for the opportunity to gain real-world experience at Kapitalbank.

Overall, the internship was completed successfully. The students demonstrated responsibility, teamwork, and a strong willingness to learn. The practical experience gained during the internship will help them in their future professional careers in banking, finance, and business development.

shortReport.title: Trip to Coca Cola
shortReport.description:
Report on Educational Visit to Coca-Cola İçecek (CCI), Samarkand
Led by: Jakhongir Farkhodov
Date: 8 May 2026
On 8 May 2026, students of Samarkand International University of Technology participated in an educational field trip to the Coca-Cola İçecek (CCI) production facility located in Jambay District, Samarkand. On June 16, 2026, students from the Samarkand International University of Technology (SIUT) visited the Samarkand Regional Territorial Department of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCI) of Uzbekistan. •
Protection of entrepreneurs' rights: participating in inspections, providing legal support, and representing business interests in court.
•
Support and training: running business incubators, providing consulting services, and improving the skills of workers.

On June 18, 2026, students from the Samarkand International University of Technology (SIUT) visited Samarkand International Airport. This is the first airport in the modern history of Uzbekistan built from scratch through a public-private partnership, led by investor Bakhtiyor Fazylov.
Structure and Management The project was realized through an agreement between "AIR MARAKANDA," which manages the new terminal and ground services, and the state partner, "Uzbekistan Airports."

Terminal: The total area is 40,700 square meters. The design is based on the work of Mirzo Ulugbek, "New Astronomical Tables," and the building is shaped like an open book.

Services: The airport meets international standards and is accessible for passengers with limited mobility. There is a capsule hotel, a luggage wrapping service, and VIP and CIP lounges.

Secondary source: Aviation expenses related to passenger transport.

shortReport.title: Career Launch Essentials - Self Awareness
shortReport.description:
The students were equipped with tools to understand their strengths, weaknesses, and how to best communicate these to potential employers in future. This forms the foundation for their resume writing and job interviews in future. More importantly, it primes them to recognise how best to market themselves as a 'personal brand' that would make themselves appealing for a job recruiter (and get hired). 

The implications of having low self awareness was discussed, and we spoke about how to rectify this. A case study was given to them and the students suggested ways to address the problem in the case study. 

There were also 3 problem stations that was given to them, to help them understand "Analytical problems", "Creative Problems", and "Social Problems". This helps the students recognise the kind of problems they gravitate to, and learn how to solve them. The students learnt that being astute problem solvers make them highly employable in future. 

Communication tools were also imparted through hands-on activities and practices, and the students got to try asking good questions and answering them effectively.

shortReport.title: Career Launch Essentials: Values and Resume Writing
shortReport.description:
The students identified what their values were today and recognised what was important to them when it came to career directions. They learnt that values were like a compass for them. More importantly, they were grouped up and challenged to communicate what these values were and how it helped them stand out as individuals. This is based on the lesson that they need toclearly communicate strengths, direction and values.

We also imparted to the students that internships and careers should be something that they own for themselves, and not always rely on others to get for them. It is ultimately the individual's responsibility to learn beyond the classroom. This was reinforced through an activity: The 100 Opportunities list. 

Lastly, the students started to write their resumes, and learnt to develop what works best for them to be in a more hireable position. They were also tasked to 'edit' each other's work, so that the lesson can be reinforced.

shortReport.title: Applied Math for Design
shortReport.description:
The students started their foundational math class today, in anticipation of their possible roles in industrial design spheres / interior design spheres that would need basic mathematical understanding. The REI Summer Interns took them for this class, and gave the students a diagnostic test to ascertain their math proficiencies. This is to give us an idea of where the students are at with certain mathematical concepts and levels, and to inform us what we should cover more in detail over the remaining days of the in-house internship. 

The session ended with a class on some of the specific questions that most of the students got wrong, as an introduction to the mathematical concept. This is so that the students will get an initial understanding of the concepts and why they got the questions wrong.

shortReport.title: Applied Mathematics: Budgeting and Measurements for Design
shortReport.description:
On the second day of the students’ foundational math class, two REI Summer Interns took the lead in teaching the lesson. The class began with a worksheet focused on algebraic equations that were similar to the diagnostic exam the students completed the previous day. During this activity, students reviewed multiplying and dividing fractions, factoring expressions, solving equations with variables, and solving systems of equations.

For the second activity, the students participated in a Kahoot review game that covered concepts from the diagnostic exam and additional topics, such as mathematical terms in English.

For the final activity, students completed a comprehensive real-world problem in which they were given a budget and an apartment layout with limited space. Their task was to design the apartment layout, including room arrangements, furniture, and other items, while staying within the assigned budget. This activity helped students strengthen their understanding of budgeting, unit conversions, ratios, and creative design thinking, while also encouraging teamwork and problem-solving.

This helped the students apply mathematical concepts in design scenarios, something that they might need for work in future.

shortReport.title: Applied Math for Design: Graphs
shortReport.description:
The in house internship began with a lecture and worksheet focused on graphing linear equations in slope-intercept form and graphing quadratic functions. Graphs are important for students, when they need to research and make sense of data for strategic user surveys and feedback. 

A game was also played for students to revise what they have learnt. They were divided into two teams and each team was given an equation to graph. This went on for a few rounds to ensure that they understood core principles of graphing, and to confidently apply what they learnt. 

For the final activity, students played Kahoot to review the material covered on the final exam. The REI interns would step in whenever a significant number of students struggled with a concept and walk them through the process of solving it.

shortReport.title: Applied Math: TRIGONOMETRY
shortReport.description:
On the fourth day of the students' foundational mathematics course, the two REI summer interns led a lesson focused on trigonometry concepts covered on the exam. The session began with a lecture introducing the unit circle, trigonometric functions, and the Pythagorean Theorem. Following the lecture, students completed a worksheet designed to reinforce and apply the concepts they had just learned.

The second activity featured a team-based competition in which the girls and boys competed to solve trigonometry problems. Students were encouraged to collaborate and communicate with their teammates, fostering peer learning and active engagement with the material.

For the final activity, students worked through a comprehensive real-world trigonometry problem. They were tasked with determining the optimal ladder length needed to rescue an individual from a burning building, allowing them to apply trigonometric principles in a practical, problem-solving context.

shortReport.title: Applied Math for Design: Foundational Math
shortReport.description:
On the final day of the students' foundational mathematics course, the interns did their post-course diagnostic exam. To reinforce the concepts covered throughout the week, students participated in an interactive Kahoot review that addressed all of the major topics featured on the assessment.

Following the review session, students completed the diagnostic exam that they had originally taken on the first day of the course. The results demonstrated significant improvement across the class. The average score increased from 35% on Day 1 to 62% on the final day, representing a 27-percentage-point gain in just five days. Several students showed particularly remarkable growth, highlighting the effectiveness of the instruction and their dedication to learning. 

Overall, the course proved to be highly beneficial for the design students. In addition to strengthening their mathematical foundations, the curriculum emphasized practical, real-world applications, enabling students to better understand how these concepts can be applied beyond the classroom.
