shortReport.title: Activities Conducted on the Fifth Day of the Internship at Navobod Naslli Parranda
shortReport.description:
On June 5, 2026, students participating in the INTERNSHIP-2026 program at Navobod Naslli Parranda continued their practical training by engaging in activities related to accounting, electronic document management, logistics documentation, and freight forwarding operations. The fifth day provided students with valuable exposure to the administrative and logistical processes that support the efficient functioning of the enterprise.

During the internship, student Dilfuza Kamoliddinova worked in the Accounting Department, where she gained practical experience with the enterprise’s electronic document management system, Didox. Throughout the day, she reviewed and processed various financial documents, including invoices and supporting accounting records. She learned how to monitor document statuses, verify financial information, and organize documentation within a digital environment. This experience enabled her to better understand the role of electronic document management systems in modern business operations and financial administration.

In addition to accounting-related activities, students were introduced to the preparation and verification of waybills used in transportation and logistics operations. They learned how to complete essential sections of transport documentation, including information about the sender, receiver, type of goods, quantities, and delivery details. Special attention was given to checking the accuracy and completeness of documents before shipment. Through this activity, students gained a deeper understanding of the importance of proper documentation in ensuring efficient logistics processes and regulatory compliance.

Student Asrorova Adiba continued to develop her knowledge of business documentation and operational procedures. During the day, she observed how transportation and commercial documents are coordinated with enterprise activities and how accurate record-keeping contributes to effective communication between departments and external partners.

Furthermore, students Muxtarov Fazli Furkatovich, Nasimov Damir Zoirovich, and Kendjayev Timur Murodkulovich participated in logistics-related assignments associated with freight forwarding operations. Under the supervision of enterprise specialists, they studied the procedures for preparing shipping documentation required for the transportation of goods. They became familiar with the documentation flow used in freight forwarding, including shipment records, transport instructions, and supporting logistics documents. This practical experience enhanced their understanding of supply chain operations and transportation management practices.

Throughout the day, supervisors emphasized the importance of accuracy, responsibility, and attention to detail when handling accounting and logistics documentation. Students were encouraged to apply theoretical concepts acquired at the university to real business situations and to understand the critical role that documentation plays in supporting enterprise activities.

The practical tasks completed during the fifth day strengthened students’ competencies in accounting administration, digital document management, transportation documentation, and logistics coordination. These experiences allowed them to gain valuable professional skills that are directly applicable in modern business and industrial environments.

Conclusion

The fifth day of the internship at Navobod Naslli Parranda provided students with meaningful practical experience in accounting and logistics operations. Through their involvement in electronic document management, invoice processing, waybill preparation, and freight forwarding documentation, students developed a stronger understanding of administrative procedures and supply chain management. The knowledge and skills gained during the day contributed significantly to their professional development and preparedness for future careers in business, accounting, and logistics.

shortReport.title: Activities Conducted on the First Day of the Internship

name: Creative Engineering Center - Group 1
plan:
**INTENSIVE LAB COURSES ON**
 
INTRODUCTION TO  ELECTROMAGNETISM

During their academic year, the 1st-year students of EPE department under CIEP have not had the opportunity to be acquainted with the fundamentals of electrical engineering, namely the concepts of electromagnetism, which should be taught within Physics-II course. Since Electrical engineering related disciplines, especially the practical aspects of it, are by far the most crucial part of their degree, the structure of the 5-day internship was constructed in the following manner:

I.	The main emphasis was made to introduce to the students to the most critical concepts of electromagnetism, including Electrostatics, Electric Charge, Capacitance, Inductance, Magnetostatics, Electric Potential (Voltage); Electric current (I); Resistance (R); Power (Watt), Magnetic Field; Permanent Magnet; Electromagnet; Direct Current (DC); Alternating Current (AC); Faraday’s Electromagnetic Induction Law; Lenz’s Law; Inductor; Transformer; transformer windings (primary/secondary); Voltage step-up/step-down with transformer; Capacitor (film capacitor and Electrolytic); Electrochemical Battery; Electromagnetic Waves; Electromagnetic/Light Spectrum; Photovoltaic Effect; Diode; AC to DC rectification with diodes and with diode bridge; Light Emitting Diode; Transistors; Power conversion principle of light to electrical energy and vice versa, Working principle of Electric Motors and Generators (power conversion between mechanical and electrical energies), Electrical Power Transmission basics, Single-phase, 2-phase, 3-phase power, Series/Parallel connections of Power sources, resistors, capacitors, inductors, solar cells; Inverter (DC/AC); Converter (DC/DC).

II.	Due to the limitation of time, maximum effort was made to visual explanation of the concepts through presentations, demonstrations of the effects through variety of experimental setups in the classrooms, and simple hands-on activities by the students.

III.	Every single demonstration of each concept, included the usage of commercially available parts or products, or instruments, so that the students will be exposed to real-life applications of each concept.

shortReport.title: Day-1. Electrostatics, Electric Charge, Electric Potential
shortReport.description:
Key concepts of Electrostatics were introduced, including:
Electric charge, basic Atomic structure, Valence electrons, Ions, Coulomb's Law, Conductors (solid, liquid and plasma), Insulators, Metals, Electric fields.
Main effort was made to introduce all types of Potential energy through demonstrations, so that specifically the concepts of Electric Potential, would be remembered by the students through analogies. To that end, the concepts of Gravitational potential, Elastic potential, Chemical potential, Pressure differential, Heat differential were demonstrated with multiple examples.
Then the concepts of Electric Potential, Voltage, Constant Voltage sources, Batteries, Photovoltaic cell, Controllable Voltage source, chargers with constant voltage output were introduced through examples.
Measurement instruments, such as Digital multimeter, Oscilloscope, Arbitrary Waveform Generator, were introduced, and the students made the voltage measurements of series and parallel connected batteries, and continuity tests with multimeters.
Concepts of changing voltage, including sinewave, square-wave and impulse voltage shapes, and the concepts of frequency were introduced, and demonstrated visually on the oscilloscope, while using LEDs.

shortReport.title: Day-2. Electric Current, Resistance, Ohm's Law, Electric Power
shortReport.description:
Key aspects of Electric current were introduced, including:
Units of measurements, actual current measurements via demonstrations, and analogies. etc.
The concept of Resistance was introduced, with multiple analogies from air movement through pressure vessel, etc. Multiple demonstrations of resistances in the electric circuits were demonstrated with different metals and resistors.
Ohm’s Law and the relationships among Voltage, Current, and Resistance were thoroughly explained via presentation slides and demonstrated with multiple real-life examples.
Joule heating effect in resistive elements in the electric circuits was demonstrated with 7 examples.
Effects of connecting resistances in series and in parallel was explained and demonstrated with multiple examples in real electrical circuits.
Ohmic (linear) and non-ohmic resistance types were explained and demonstrated with (1) linear high-power resistance I-V curve, (b) Light bulb’s I-V curve, and (c) high power LED array’s I-V curve.
Concept of Electric Power was introduced, and demonstrated with over 10 examples and measurements.
In addition to demonstrating electric power measurement at common voltage and current level appliances (10V-220V, and 0.1A-20A) high-voltage low-current (30KV, 0.02A) plasma generating device’s was compared to low-voltage high-current (20V, 200A) welding machine (which is also another form of plasma). Thermal and Optical effects, as well as current conducting behavior of high-current plasma was demonstrated with real welding machine. The students were given eye protecting darkened glasses for safety purposes.
Energy efficiency levels, as well as electricity to light conversion efficiencies  were demonstrated for incandescent lamp (150W) and LED array (150W in total). The students calculated power consumption levels by taking measurements of both lighting demonstrations.
Internal Resistance concept for Constant Voltage Sources was explained and demonstrated with multiple examples, including different capacity batteries and power supplies.
The concept of short circuit was introduced and demonstrated.
The students were given multiple tasks during the class, including taking simple measurements of voltages and currents, and calculating power levels while connecting different resistances in the circuits.

shortReport.title: Day 3
shortReport.description:
Day-3. Magnetostatics, Permanent Magnet, Electromagnet, Magnetic materials, Electric Motor
Key aspects of static magnetism were introduced, including:
Magnetic field lines, poles, 2D and 3D models of magnetic field lines of permanent magnet, Earth’s magnetic poles, 3 types of magnetism (diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic material properties were explained with demonstrations).
Magnetic properties of Electron and Magnetic domains of Ferromagnets were explained. Curie temperature of ferromagnetic material was demonstrated with real life example (by heating magnetically levitated bolt, which loses its strong magnetic properties at specific temperature). Soft vs Hard magnetic materials were explained with examples (soft iron, electrical steel, vs ceramic and neodymium permanent magnets).
Magnetic field around a single current conducting wire were explained and demonstrated with compasses made out of needles on hard paper floating on water around a conductor.
Magnetic field shape is explained and demonstrated with a single loop of high current conducting wire. Magnetic field of multiple a multi-turn air-core coils is shown to the students.
Magnetic strength of electromagnetic coils with different sized cylindrical iron cores, as well as with different number of turns and wire gauges were demonstrated.
Lack of external magnetic field of a single wire electromagnet with completely closed magnetic circuit (iron ring washers around the wire) was demonstrated to highlight the properties of magnetic fields.
Magnetic field strength of large E-core electromagnet is demonstrated by closing the magnetic circuit with external iron material.
Lorenz’s force was demonstrated by the effect of magnetic field of a permanent magnet on high voltage plasma.
Automotive solenoid used in fuel supply system of internal combustion engine cars was demonstrated as an example.
Different types of high current Relays and Contactors, which use electromagnets to make/break contacts, were shown, explained and demonstrated.
Work of a brushed (DC) electric motor was explained, step-by-step, with multiple disassembled real-life motors.
Different topologies (with permanent magnets, or electromagnets, on the rotor or on the stator) of brushed motors were demonstrated.

shortReport.title: Day-4. Alternating Current, Electromagnetic Induction, Electric Generator, 3-phase Power, Electric Transformer, Asynchronous Induction Motor, Inductive heating
shortReport.description:
Law of Electromagnetic Induction, i.e. appearance of induced voltage/current on a coil, by externally changing magnetic field, was explained, and demonstrated with part of the pieces of the real permanent magnet generator prototype that has been assembled in previous internship season.
Faraday’s Law, and Lenz’s law were explained in detail with formulas and electromechanical examples.
Sinusoidal voltage/current waveform resulting from mechanically rotating magnetic field was explained with analogies, and the concept of frequency is explained in more detail.
Principles of electricity generation by electromechanical means (via electric generators) have been explained step-by-step with conceptual pictures/animations and real-life pictures of parts of synchronous 3-phase industrial generators.
Different types of electric generators, with their application fields was explained.
Critical importance of electric generators for the global civilization was explained with examples, charts and statistics.
Concept of self-inductance and inductor in an AC circuit was explained, and the behavior of the inductor in the real electric circuit was demonstrated.
The concept of electric transformer was introduced, and the principle of operation was demonstrated using real transformer in DC and AC current cases.
Voltage stepping-up and stepping-down capabilities of the transformers, also their circuit isolation properties were explained in detail and demonstrated with 5 examples.
Analogies between the transformer and gears/levers were explained, and demonstrated with examples.
Working principle of Induction heating was explained in details and demonstrated with real example (low power HF induction heater).
Working principle of Asynchronous Electric motor was explained and demonstrated with the parts of real motor.

shortReport.title: Day-5. Capacitance
shortReport.description:
The concept of Capacitance was introduced in detail.
First simple atomic explanation was given, then the concept was demonstrated by applying high voltage to parallel foils separated by insulating paper (used in industrial transformers and motors). Electrostatic forces on the foils, made visible, so that the students could have intuitive idea about the separation of opposite charges.
Geometric aspects of a capacitor were explained, then demonstrated by taking measurements of different kinds of film capacitors, then the students were made to disassemble real capacitors to have better understanding of the structure of real capacitors.
Charge storage properties of capacitors were explained and demonstrated.
The internal structure and working principle of electrolytic capacitors is explained, and one electrolytic capacitor is disassembled for demonstration.
Charging and discharging of capacitors was demonstrated with capacitors connected in series and in parallel.
Measurements were taken with series and parallel connected capacitors.
Safety aspects of charged capacitors were explained and demonstrated with charging and discharging a large high voltage capacitor bank.
Dielectric properties of materials were introduced, and different capacitor types were shown and explained (including ceramic, film, metallized foil, electrolytic, air-gap, vacuum, de-ionized water based, etc.).
The properties of capacitors in DC and AC circuits is explained and demonstrated.

name: Creative Engineering Center - Group 2
plan:
INTENSIVE LAB COURSES ON 
INTRODUCTION TO POWER CONVERTERS
During their academic year, the 2nd-year and 3-rd year students of Renewable Energy department KITC had the opportunity to familiarize themselves with the fundamentals of electromagnetism, including the theoretical and practical aspects of key concepts which are the building blocks of Electrical Engineering. That included:
I.	Electrostatics, Electric Charge, Electric Potential (Voltage); Electric current (I); Resistance (R); Power (Watt); Magnetostatics, Permanent Magnet & Electromagnet; Direct Current (DC); Alternating Current (AC); Faraday’s Electromagnetic Induction Law; Lenz’s Law; Inductor; Transformer; Capacitor; Electromagnetic Waves; Electromagnetic/Light Spectrum; Photovoltaic Effect; Series/Parallel connections of Power sources, resistors, capacitors, inductors, solar cells; Basic principle of Electrochemical battery, etc.
II.	Working principle of Electric Motors and Generators (power conversion between mechanical and electrical energies), Electrical Power Transmission basics, Single-phase, 2-phase, 3-phase power, etc.
III.	Surface level introduction to semiconductors.
In order to advance the knowledge and understanding of the RE students in the field of Electrical Engineering one step further, the main emphasis for the 2-week summer internship of 2026 year, will be made on the following areas:
1.	Deeper introduction to semiconductor technology, with special focus on Power Electronics;
2.	Introduction to Power Converters, including Rectifiers (AC/DC); Inverters (DC/AC), , DC-DC converter classes;
3.	Working principle of key semiconductor technologies used in Power converters, including important types of diodes, transistors.
4.	Introduction to Power converters architecture, including Power switching devices, driver circuits, control circuits.
5.	Introduction to Power Amplifiers, and Amplifier classes, with main emphasis on Class-D topologies.
6.	Most common power converter topologies, Half-bridge, Full-bridge, Push-Pull, etc.
Due to the limitation of time, and extremely broad scope of the topics to be covered, maximum effort was made to visual explanation of the concepts through presentations, demonstrations of the effects through variety of experimental setups in the classrooms, and simple hands-on activities by the students.
Every single demonstration of each concept, included the usage of commercially available parts or products, or instruments, so that the students will be exposed to real-life applications of each concept.

shortReport.title: Day-1. Introduction to Semiconductors & the overview of their use as Power Converters in electricity demand side
shortReport.description:
The first day of the internship was dedicated to familiarize the students with overall plan of the 2-week internship course, namely the focus on semiconductors used in Power Electronics and more specifically in Power Converter technologies.
I.	The most critical aspects of global electricity generation technology were reviewed, as a refresher. Then classification of power (electricity) consumption is introduced. Extreme importance of power conversion technology at electricity consumption side is explained with multiple examples. Important forms and waveforms of power supply are explained, including DC, Sinusoidal AC, Square wave, Pulsed DC, PWM, etc. Importance of Semiconductor technologies as switching technology is described through analogies of mechanical/hand-controlled switches, relays, electromagnetic contactors, etc.
II.	Block diagrams of fundamental power converters, and their classifications is introduced, including types of AC/DC, DC/AC, DC/DC converters and their subcategories.
III.	Theoretical aspects of Semiconductors are explained, starting from atomics structure of elements, going through concepts of valence electrons, conductors, insulators, up to creating doped materials which make the basic building block of PN junction.
IV.	The structure of PN junction of semiconductor devices is explained in more detail, then the concept of diode is introduced in more details. Behavior of basic diode is explained. Different types of diodes and the devices behaving like the diodes is introduced, including, rectifying diodes, Schottky diodes, LEDs, PV cells, Zener diodes, etc. Different types of real diodes were shown to the students, and the behavior of some were demonstrated. Key parameters of diodes, as well as series-parallel connection possibilities of the latter were explained, and shown by examples.

shortReport.title: Day-2. Diodes, Diode based Rectifiers, (AC/DC converters)
shortReport.description:
Basic working principle of diodes is explained, and demonstrated with multiple examples in DC circuit conditions.
Non-Ohmic behavior of diodes is compared to pure resistive elements (with pure ohmic behavior), as well as to non-ohmic heating elements in the example of incandescent light bulb.
The forward voltage drop aspect of diode is explained and demonstrated. Reverse voltage blocking is explained and demonstrated.
Forward current conducting limitations and reverse breakdown limitations of rectifier diode is explained in DC circuit conditions.
10A 1000V rated rectifier diode is broken up to let the students see the internal structure of a diode.
Single diode’s behavior in sinusoidal alternating current is explained and demonstrated at mains voltage and frequency (50Hz), and at higher frequencies.
Diode bridge (4-diodes) full-wave rectification is explained and demonstrated. 
Role of rectifying capacitor in relation to diodes is explained and demonstrated with multiple capacitor values and in different load conditions.
Center-tapped transformer based 2-diode full-wave rectification is explained and demonstrated at 50Hz.
The students were divided into 2 groups and built and tested simple AC-DC rectifier based on diode bridge circuit.

shortReport.title: Day-3. Rectifier circuits inside Welding machine. Zener Diodes, Bipolar Junction Transistors, and MOSFETs
shortReport.description:
To enforce the knowledge gained by the students on the previous lesson, especially the AC/DC conversion or voltage rectification topologies using diodes, the students were made to disassemble the major parts of a real welding machine, with 200A current output capacity. The students saw, real world application of voltage rectification both at the power input side of the welding machine circuit, as well as at the output of the machine. Voltage waveform (DC) at the output of a welding machine was shown to the students with the oscilloscope. Then, after the students reassembled the welding machine, the welding process was demonstrated with plasma arc (with safety glasses on for each student), shortly, to explain how the modern welding machines convert the main’s power (220Vrms, single phase, 50Hz), to 27Vdc/20A-200A output, through AC/DC – DC/AC – AC/DC converters.
Working principle of Zener diodes was explained, including the IV curve of Zener diodes in forward and revere bias conditions. Real world Zener diode types (1 watt and 2 watt versions with multiple reverse bias voltage ratings, including 5V, 12V, 18V, 20V, 23V), were shown to the students.
Working principle of Zener diodes, especially voltage clipping function, was demonstrated with signal generator, oscilloscope, and step-up transformer, in sinusoidal signal conditions at different frequencies.
Use cases of anti-parallel series connected Zener diode pairs, was explained and demonstrated.
Zener diode’s use as Voltage reference device for low power signals, was explained and demonstrated.
Then, basic structure of Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT) was introduced to the students, and its working principle as a switch was explained with a presentation and a short Youtube video. Then a real switching behavior of a BJT was demonstrated in DC circuit conditions, where small incandescent lightbulb (5W, 24V), was switched on and off using series connected small power NPN BJT transistor (in TO-220). Differences between NPN and PNP BJTs were explained with slides.
Then, Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect-Transistor (MOSFET) was introduced briefly, and its working principle as a switch, as well as its different behavior compared to BJT, was explained and demonstrated, in DC circuit conditions.
The switching behavior of the power MOSFET (in TO-247 package), was demonstrated, using DC power supply, incandescent small lightbulb, signal generator for controlling the MOSFET gate, and the oscilloscope. The demonstration was made in such a way, that the students would visually see the lightbulb blinking at low frequencies (1Hz-4Hz), while being switched on and off by the series connected MOSFET, and they could see the voltage waveform (squarewave) at high frequency switched conditions (1kHz), at the oscilloscope, while the lightbulb would output seemingly constant light output with lower brightness.

shortReport.title: Day-6. Types of Power switches. Introduction to Gate drivers
shortReport.description:
The most widely used transistor types, namely BJT, MOSFET, IGBT and Thyristor, that are used as power switches; their key properties and basic structures, wered described in presentation form. Advantages and disadvantages of each type of transistor and their most common application fields are explained.
The block diagram of control circuitry of power switches was introduced. Including (1) Control signal generation block (Microcontroller, PWM or Logic level signal generator), (2) Gate driver circuit, when necessary (3) signal amplifying Interface circuit between logic level control block and driver circuit, and (4) Interface circuit or amplifier between the Gate driver circuit and high-power switch gates.
Fundamental role of control signal generation block for switching the power transistors, as well as the associated circuits that allow microcontroller units (MCU) chips or small signal generating integrated circuits (IC) to operate, were explained to the students. Examples of MCUs and other ICs were shown to the students with real world converter circuits. Input power requirements for the ICs and MCUs, as well as current and voltage supply limitations of ICs and MCUs with regards to driving the power switches was explained.
Critical role of Gate driver circuits, as an amplifying stage between low power signal generators and power switch gates, was explained. Input power requirements for the Gate drivers was explained. Major types of MOSFET and IGBT gate drivers was described. In particular, the difference between isolated and non-isolated gate drivers was explained. Working principle of Optically isolated drivers, Gate Drive Transformers (GDT) was explained.
Working of GDT driven MOSFET was demonstrated using, real MOSFET, Signal generator, Oscilloscope, benchtop DC power supply (32V/5A), high power LED arrays (as load). Power LED array circuit was operated at medium frequencies (50 kHz – 100kHz), with varying duty cycles (1%-50%).
To enforce the knowledge gained by the students on the previous lesson, the students were made to disassemble and reassemble the major circuit blocks of a real pure sinewave DC/AC inverter, with 1200W power output capacity, in order to see the examples of control signal block, gate drivers and power MOSFETS.
Parallel connected high power IGBT array (8 transistors in TO-247 package) circuit in push-pull topology was shown as an example of a power circuit. Low frequency gate drive transformer, specifically designed to drive those IGBTs was shown and its parameters were explained in detail.
Importance and advantages of high-frequency power converters was explained with the pictures of real-world converters. Key aspects of size reduction in capacitors, and especially inductors and transformers at high-frequencies, was explained and shown with real examples.

shortReport.title: Day-7. RC, RL, LC circuits, Resonant circuits, Half-Bridge, Push-Pull inverter topologies
shortReport.description:
Passive electronics and electrical components, in particular, (resistors, capacitors, inductors, and transformer), including the theory of their working principles, were reviewed. Energy storage properties of capacitors and inductors in general and their use in power converters, in particular were explained.
The behavior of combined elements, namely, Resistor-Capacitor (RC), Resistor-Inductor (RL), as well as Inductor-Capacitor (LC), were explained in detail with presentation slides, and demonstrated using the real components, power supply unit, the signal generator and an oscilloscope. Growing importance of converter topologies using LC resonance, and the advantages of using resonant effects in high-frequency high-efficiency converters was explained. Behavior of series and parallel LC circuits were demonstrated with signal generator and oscilloscope.
The most basic topologies of converters (Buck, Boost, Buck-Boost), which employ single active switching device, single diode, single inductive element, and a single capacitive element.
Working principle of Half-bridge, Full-Bridge and Push-Pull Inverter topologies was explained.
Push-pull topology was chosen for the high-power stage of the medium/low frequency inverter circuit, which is the final project of the internship. High-power stage of the inverter consisted of 8 IGBT transistors, (4 transistors connected in parallel on each leg of the Push-Pull circuit), 2 Zener diodes for each leg of the push-pull for gate protection, heat sinks, 2 current limiting inductors. That part of the inverter circuit was preassembled by the tutor to save time for the students, as it required more careful layout and longer time to assemble. The power stage was designed with a goal to convert DC output coming out of a rectified Mains supply voltage (310Vdc), and the transistors with the capacity to handle up to 1200V reverse voltage.
Half-bridge topology was chosen for the simple gate driver transformer (GDT) controlled, Gate Driver, which in its turn should drive the high-power stage with a GDT.
Power supply for the Gate Driver, as well as the small-signal control circuit, was decided to be taken directly from the main voltage supply of the high-power stage, by stepping down the voltage, using resistive voltage dividers, and regulating it with Zener diodes and capacitors.

shortReport.title: Day-8. Printed circuit board (PCB), Soldering process and techniques.
shortReport.description:
Structure of Printed Circuit Board (PCB), their manufacturing process, the main PCB types, and their advantages was explained, and demonstrated with Youtube videos, and real-world circuits.
The process of soldering electronics components was explained in detail. Each critical soldering element, including the flux and its types (that protects the solder from oxidation), solder wire and its types, soldering iron types and its tips, tip cleaning pad, tip cleaning wire mesh, flux removal alcohol (isopropyl), were explained. Optimal and non-optimal soldering nuances, including temperature control, bonding methods, through hole and surface mount (SMD) components soldering, were explained and shown on real-world circuit boards.
The students tried soldering different wires together, and also soldering wires to through hole circuit boards. The strength and quality of the solder bond was tested mechanically and visually.

shortReport.title: Day-9. Design of Gate-Driver circuit and component selection exercise
shortReport.description:
The main exercise around assembling the medium-frequency, medium-power inverter, with the students, was centered around designing and assembling the Gate driver circuit, which is the interface between the high-power stage and small-signal control circuit.
The Gate driver for the inverter was designed in such a way that all the components would be visible, understandable, and easy to work with for the students. Therefore, using off-the-shelf small gate driver IC was avoided. Due to the relatively low-frequency operation of the inverter (800Hz-40kHz), the gates of the Driver transistors, as well as the output of the Driver circuit used transformers of considerably larger size than the gate-driver transformers (GDT) used in real-world applications. 
The goal from this exercise was to make the students understand the most critical function of the gate driver circuit, namely, charging and discharging gate capacitances of large MOSFETs and IGBTs at highest possible speeds at a given frequency, and ensuring the proper isolation of driving/controlling side, from the high-voltage high-power stage.
The students were engaged in component selection exercise for the Gate Driver, as well as for the optimal layout of the components on the through hole circuit board before soldering.
The students were shown different circuit drawings of half-bridge topologies, and they were taught to recognize the circuit components on the schematics.
The students were taught how to search for and use the Datasheets of different electronics components, how to select transistors, Zener diodes, short-circuit protection fuse, capacitors, transformers, etc.
Comprehensive nature of technical information on the Datasheet of modern transistors was shown and explained in the example of SiC MOSFET.

shortReport.title: Day-13.  Testing the assembled Gate Driver circuit with the Inverter
shortReport.description:
Once the assembly process of all the components of the key blocks of the inverter was completed, final assembly of the blocks, and the testing the proper functioning of each block was started. Every single following connections were either made or tested together with the students.
Original power supply was taken from 12V lead-acid car battery. Then the DC output of the battery was converted to AC via commercial 1200W pure sinewave inverter, with 220Vrms 50Hz output. The power for the inverter circuit made with the students were taken out of the inverter.
First, AC output of commercial inverter was rectified with 4 high power diodes (1000V, 80A each) connected in diode bridge mode, then smoothed with 2 parallel connected electrolytic capacitors (450V 470uF each). 
DC output, taken after the AC/DC conversion (310V DC), was supplied via a manual switch, to the high-power block of the inverter, which consisted of 2 current limiting inductors with ferrite cores connected to the two legs of the push-pull topology, each leg of which consisted of 4, 1200V IGBT transistors. The high-power block was designed to drive tank circuit, air-core inductor of which was designed to work as the working coil of induction heater.
310V DC output was also directly connected to the control and Gate Driver blocks, through voltage divider and voltage referencing circuit (made of resistors, zener diodes and capacitors), which was designed to provide 20V dc both to Gate driver and the Control circuit.
Gate driver circuit was build on the basis of half-bridge topology, using two low gate capacitance 60V MOSFETs, Gate driver transformer, both at the controlling side and on the output side.
Control circuit or small signal generator function of the inverter was done first by commercially available PWM circuit (ZK-PP1K), then by custom made Mazilli ZVS driver/oscillator.
Since the maximum power level of the inverter was above 1kW, strict precautions were taken to ensure safety of the students and the circuits.

At 2:00 PM, we were picked up from the dormitory and taken to the main building’s office. There, we received a safety instruction on how to behave if we encountered wild animals, as well as what to do if we were attacked. We learned how to distinguish venomous snakes from non-venomous ones and studied the symptoms and types of poisons. After the lecture, we walked through the animals’ natural habitat. We returned to the canteen for dinner at 6:00 PM. After dinner, everyone went back to their rooms to rest.

shortReport.title: Day 2 – June 3, 2026: Environmental Tour and Wind Turbine Basics
shortReport.description:
On June 3, 2026, we gathered at 8:00 AM and went to the canteen for breakfast. Afterwards, we were asked to assemble at 9:30 AM for a trip to explore the surrounding environment and visit the wind turbines. We successfully reached the wind turbines and walked through the steppe.

We returned to the dormitory at 11:30 AM. After lunch, we waited until 2:00 PM for a lecture. Today’s lecture covered wind turbines: what they are made of and their operating principles. At the end of the lesson, we each made small rotor models of wind turbines by hand. After the lecture, we returned to the canteen, and following dinner, everyone went back to rest.

shortReport.title: Day 3 – June 4, 2026: Turbine Construction and PPE Practical
shortReport.description:
On June 4, 2026, we assembled at 9:00 AM in the main building’s office for a lecture that continued the topic of wind turbines. In this session, we learned how all the parts of a wind turbine are created, how the soil and foundation are prepared for installation, the internal layout of a turbine, what components are inside and their purposes, and why turbines have three blades.

After lunch at 2:00 PM, we returned to the main building, where we received an instruction on PPE (Personal Protective Equipment). We studied the theory and then proceeded to a test area with the necessary conditions. There, we put on all the required gear and performed a climb to a height of 5 meters, following all instructions under the guidance of experienced professionals.

shortReport.title: Day 4 – June 5, 2026: Advanced PPE, Safety Statistics, and Emergency Procedures
shortReport.description:
On the morning of June 5, 2026, we gathered at 9:00 AM in the main building. We continued the lecture on types of PPE, how to secure ourselves, which protective equipment has an expiration date, and their specific purposes. We also studied statistics on the most common workplace incidents and their fatality probabilities.

After lunch at 2:00 PM, we returned to continue the PPE topic, where we learned what to do in emergency situations — for example, how to exit a wind turbine during a fire and how to rescue a person who has lost consciousness inside the generator. After the lecture ended, we returned to the dormitory and continued resting.

shortReport.title: Day 5 – June 6, 2026: Trip to Lake Ayakagytma and Departure
shortReport.description:
On the morning of June 6, 2026, we were asked to gather at 8:30 AM. We all assembled, got into the vehicle, and drove to Lake Ayakagytma. This lake is located not far from the power plant. The journey to the lake took approximately 30 to 45 minutes.

Upon arriving at the lake, we were told about it — why the ground beneath us is so soft and why there are salt streaks on the sand. The lake is located in the Bukhara region, Gijduvan district. After documenting our arrival at the lake, we headed back to the power plant. Before departure, we had been told in advance to tidy our rooms and pack all our belongings so as not to be late for the meeting. We returned to the dormitory, collected our things, and left the power plant.


Overall Impression
The five days we spent at the wind power plant went very well and were truly memorable. We liked everything — the instructors, the lectures, the practical sessions, and the conditions provided to us. Everything was of the highest standard.

1. Arrival and Reception
On the evening of June 22, the student delegation from the Chinese Institute of Electric Power at Samarkand International University of Technology departed from Uzbekistan for their summer camp program in China. After an international flight, they arrived at the Chinese campus of Northeast Electrical Power University on the evening of June 23.
Upon arrival at Jilin airport, the students were warmly welcomed by representatives of NEEPU, who had organized dedicated ground transportation to ensure a smooth and comfortable transfer to the university campus. The efficient reception set a positive tone for the days ahead.

2. Official Meeting with University Leadership – June 24
On June 24, the SIUT delegation had the honor of meeting with the President of NEEPU, along with deans, vice-deans, and department heads from various faculties. The meeting was conducted in a formal yet cordial atmosphere.
The Rector of NEEPU delivered a welcome and congratulatory address, expressing his enthusiasm for the growing academic cooperation between the two institutions and his best wishes for the students’ educational and cultural experience in China.
In response, Ms. Pak Kseniya, Senior Chinese Language Teacher at the Chinese Institute of Electric Power of SIUT, delivered a heartfelt speech of gratitude on behalf of the delegation. She thanked the NEEPU leadership and staff for their hospitality and for organizing such a comprehensive program.
The meeting concluded with a ceremonial exchange of gifts, symbolizing the strengthening friendship between Uzbekistan and China. Following the official proceedings, the students were given a guided tour of the NEEPU campus.

3. Academic and Cultural Program – June 25
Morning Session: Introduction to Energy and Power Engineering
On the morning of June 25, the students participated in their first major academic session: “Introduction to Energy and Power Engineering.” The lecture provided a foundational overview of energy systems, covering:
•	Various forms of energy: mechanical, thermal, electrical, chemical, and nuclear energy;
•	Classification of energy sources into renewable and non-renewable categories, along with basic definitions;
•	A roadmap for energy utilization, illustrating how different energy types are converted into electric power;
•	Technical explanations of the steam dynamic cycle, boiler systems, and the essential equipment used in thermal power plants.
The lecturer used diagrams and real-world examples to explain how thermal power stations operate, giving students a clear understanding of the entire energy conversion chain—from raw fuel input to electricity generation. The session was highly interactive, with students asking questions and engaging in discussions about energy efficiency and sustainability.
Afternoon Session: Chinese Language and Culture Class
In the afternoon, the students attended a Chinese language and culture class, designed to deepen their understanding of the host region and improve their practical language skills. The lesson included:
•	A detailed geographical and cultural overview of Jilin City, Jilin Province, and the nearby metropolitan center of Changchun;
•	Grammar exercises tailored to intermediate and advanced learners;
•	Interactive speaking activities that allowed students to practice and showcase their Chinese language proficiency.
The class was both educational and enjoyable, providing a balance between linguistic development and cultural immersion. Students demonstrated active participation and received positive feedback from the instructor.

shortReport.title: Friday theory and practice
shortReport.description:
1. Morning Session: In-Depth Lecture on Boiler Principles in Thermal Power Plants
The academic activities on June 26 commenced with a highly informative and detailed lecture on the principles of the boiler in thermal power plants. The session was led by an experienced NEEPU professor, who guided the students through the entire boiler operation process, from fuel input to steam generation.
Key topics covered included:
•	The role of the boiler as the primary heat-generating component in a thermal power plant;
•	Internal structure and working mechanisms, including combustion chambers, heat exchangers, and water-tube systems;
•	The coal pathway – how coal is fed into the boiler, combusted, and how the resulting ash and flue gases are managed;
•	Steam generation process – from heating water to producing high-pressure, high-temperature steam;
•	The steam-to-power chain – how the generated steam travels to the steam turbine, where it expands and produces mechanical rotational force, which is then converted into electrical energy through a generator.
The lecture was rich with diagrams, cross-sectional views, and operational data, making complex engineering concepts accessible and engaging. Students actively posed questions about combustion efficiency, emissions control, and boiler safety systems, to which the lecturer provided thorough, practical answers.

2. Afternoon Session: Laboratory Visits and Hands-On Experience
In the afternoon, the program shifted from theory to practice, as the students were given an exclusive tour of NEEPU’s specialized engineering laboratories. This hands-on segment was designed to reinforce the morning’s theoretical knowledge through direct interaction with real and simulated equipment.
a. Steam Turbine and Generator Simulator Lab
Students had the opportunity to operate a steam turbine and electricity generator simulator. This interactive setup allowed them to visualize the turbine’s rotational dynamics, adjust operational parameters, and observe in real time how changes in steam flow affect electrical output. The simulator provided a safe yet realistic environment for understanding the critical link between mechanical and electrical engineering.
b. Thermal Power Plant Layout Models
The group was then shown detailed scale models of thermal power plants. These models illustrated the complete plant layout, including the boiler house, turbine hall, cooling towers, and auxiliary systems. Professors provided hands-on explanations, pointing out each piece of equipment and describing its function within the overall system. Students were able to trace the entire energy flow path—from coal delivery to electricity dispatch—in a tangible, three-dimensional format.
c. Chemistry Lab – Coal Consistency Analysis
Following the engineering labs, the students visited a chemistry laboratory, where they participated in an experimental session on coal consistency analysis. Under the guidance of lab technicians, they learned how to assess coal quality parameters such as moisture content, ash content, and calorific value. This exercise highlighted the importance of fuel characterization in optimizing boiler performance and reducing environmental impact.
d. Introduction to Types of Thermal Energy
The students were also introduced to different types of thermal energy, including sensible heat, latent heat, and chemical heat released during combustion. The session connected thermodynamic theory with practical applications in power generation, broadening the students’ understanding of energy conversion processes.
e. Virtual Reality (VR) Lab – Immersive Power Plant Tour
The final and most memorable stop of the day was the Virtual Reality (VR) Laboratory. Using state-of-the-art VR headsets and motion-tracking systems, the students embarked on a fully immersive virtual tour of a real thermal power plant. They could walk through the boiler room, inspect turbine halls, climb up to control platforms, and observe every component in 360-degree detail—all without leaving the lab. The VR experience brought together all the knowledge from the morning lecture and afternoon demonstrations, offering a vivid, unforgettable perspective on industrial-scale energy production.

3. Summary and Reflections
The activities of June 26 proved to be a perfect blend of theoretical instruction and practical application. The morning lecture laid a solid scientific foundation, while the afternoon lab visits—including simulators, physical models, chemical analysis, and virtual reality—gave students a multidimensional understanding of thermal power plant operations.
The students expressed great enthusiasm for the VR experience in particular, noting that it helped them grasp spatial and operational relationships that are difficult to convey through textbooks alone. The chemistry lab exercise also added a valuable cross-disciplinary element, emphasizing the role of material science in energy engineering.

shortReport.title: Academic and Cultural Activities
shortReport.description:
1. Morning Session (9:30 AM) – Lecture on "Implementation of Dual Carbon Goals in China"
The academic day commenced with a timely and thought-provoking lecture on China's Dual Carbon Goals, delivered by a senior faculty member from NEEPU. The session provided a comprehensive overview of China's energy landscape, its environmental challenges, and the policy frameworks designed to address climate change.
Key Topics Covered:
•	China's Energy Situation: The lecturer began by presenting a balanced analysis of China's current energy profile. While acknowledging the country's remarkable achievements in economic growth and energy infrastructure development, the lecturer also candidly addressed negative environmental impacts resulting from rapid industrialization – including high carbon emissions, air pollution, and resource depletion. Importantly, the lecturer emphasized that China has been actively working to rectify these issues through technological innovation and policy reforms.
•	Carbon Peak and Carbon Neutrality: The core focus of the lecture was China's ambitious "Dual Carbon" policy – namely, achieving Carbon Peak by 2030 and Carbon Neutrality by 2060. The lecturer traced the historical context of these targets, explaining how domestic environmental pressures and global climate commitments shaped the government's decision to adopt such aggressive goals. The students learned about the specific milestones, sectoral strategies, and monitoring mechanisms that China has put in place to track progress toward these objectives.
•	CCUS (Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage): A significant portion of the session was dedicated to CCUS technologies. The lecturer explained how China is investing in capturing carbon emissions from industrial sources, utilizing captured CO₂ for enhanced oil recovery or chemical production, and storing it safely in geological formations. Examples of pilot projects and large-scale facilities were provided to illustrate China's practical actions in this field.
•	International Frameworks: The lecture also referenced the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, placing China's domestic policies within the broader context of global climate governance. The lecturer discussed how international obligations and cooperative efforts have influenced China's policy direction, while also highlighting China's role as a responsible major emitter committed to a green transition.
•	Climate Change Impact on Policy Formation: The lecturer concluded by explaining how observable climate change phenomena – such as extreme weather events, glacial melting, and rising sea levels – have directly influenced the Chinese government's urgency in bringing the Dual Carbon policy to the forefront of the national agenda. This segment helped students understand the real-world drivers behind high-level political decisions.
The session was highly interactive, with students posing questions about renewable energy integration, grid stability, and the economic feasibility of large-scale carbon capture. The lecturer provided detailed, evidence-based responses, making the class both informative and intellectually stimulating.
 
2. Afternoon Session (2:00 PM) – Chinese Calligraphy Workshop
The afternoon program shifted from policy to culture, offering students a hands-on introduction to the ancient art of Chinese calligraphy (书法). The workshop was not only educational but also deeply personal, as each student received a complete calligraphy set as a gift from NEEPU to take back home.
Calligraphy Kit and Opening Enthusiasm
Each student was presented with a beautifully packaged set containing:
•	A pack of high-quality calligraphy paper (rice paper);
•	Three different types of brushes (varying in size and hair type);
•	Prepared liquid ink;
•	Additional accessories such as a brush rest and felt mat.
The students expressed great excitement and sincere gratitude to the NEEPU staff and faculty for such a thoughtful and generous gift. For most participants, this was their very first experience with calligraphy, and the anticipation was palpable as they unpacked their kits.
Lecture on Chinese Characters and Calligraphy History
Before picking up their brushes, the students attended a brief lecture on the origins and evolution of Chinese characters. Key points included:
•	The philosophy behind Chinese writing – how characters evolved from pictographic representations to abstract symbols;
•	Classification of characters:
o	象形字 (Xiàngxíngzì) – pictographs that resemble physical objects (e.g., 山 for mountain, 水 for water);
o	指事字 (Zhǐshìzì) – ideographs that indicate abstract concepts (e.g., 上 for up, 下 for down);
o	会意字 (Huìyìzì) – compound characters formed by combining two or more meaningful parts (e.g., 明 – sun and moon together meaning "bright");
o	形声字 (Xíngshēngzì) – phonetic-semantic compounds, which constitute more than 80% of all Chinese characters. The lecturer explained how these characters contain a semantic radical and a phonetic component, making them more systematic and learnable.
The students also learned about the five major script styles of calligraphy in chronological order:
1.	篆书 (Zhuànshū) – Seal Script (ancient, formal, and curvilinear);
2.	隶书 (Lìshū) – Clerical Script (more structured and angular);
3.	草书 (Cǎoshū) – Cursive Script (rapid, flowing, and highly artistic);
4.	楷书 (Kǎishū) – Regular Script (standard, clear, and widely used today);
5.	行书 (Xíngshū) – Running Script (semi-cursive, balancing speed and legibility).
The instructor explained where each style is used today – from official documents and stone inscriptions to personal letters and artistic compositions – and why connoisseurs appreciate calligraphy as a profound form of visual and spiritual art.
Practical Instruction and Guided Practice
Following the theoretical introduction, students were taught the correct way to hold the brush – including grip pressure, wrist angle, and body posture. The instructor then guided them step-by-step through:
•	The basic strokes of Chinese calligraphy;
•	Proper stroke order for simple characters;
•	Techniques for controlling ink flow and brush pressure to achieve varying line thicknesses.
The teacher approached every student individually, offering personalized corrections and encouragement. This one-on-one attention ensured that even complete beginners could produce recognizable and aesthetically pleasing characters by the end of the session.
Calligraphy Contest and Homework Assignment
To add a playful competitive element, the instructor assigned slightly more complex characters and challenged the students to a friendly contest – the goal being to write the most beautiful version of the given characters. The students, now warmed up from basic practice, threw themselves into the competition with visible enthusiasm and focus. Laughter and applause filled the room as everyone admired each other's work.
At the end of the class, the teacher provided a list of additional characters for the students to practice once they return home, encouraging them to continue honing their new skill beyond the summer camp.
3. Summary and Reflections
June 29 was a day of remarkable duality – blending high-level environmental policy education with deep cultural immersion.
•	The morning lecture equipped students with a nuanced understanding of China's energy transition, its challenges, and its global significance – knowledge directly relevant to their future careers in power engineering.
•	The afternoon calligraphy workshop offered a peaceful, meditative counterpoint, allowing students to connect with Chinese aesthetics, philosophy, and craftsmanship on a personal level.
The students departed both sessions with enriched minds and grateful hearts – carrying not only new knowledge but also a tangible gift that will serve as a lasting memento of their time at NEEPU.

shortReport.title: Academic and Cultural Activities, June 30
shortReport.description:
1. Morning Session (9:30 AM) – Lecture on "Comprehensive Utilization of Biomass Technology"
The morning session featured a specialized lecture on biomass energy technology, delivered by an expert from NEEPU's energy engineering faculty. The session provided students with a thorough understanding of biomass as a renewable energy source, its conversion methods, and its strategic role in China's carbon reduction efforts.
Key Topics Covered:
•	Definition and Scope of Biomass: The lecturer began by defining biomass as organic matter derived from plants, animals, and microorganisms. Examples included agricultural residues, forestry waste, animal manure, and organic municipal solid waste. The lecturer also clarified what types of biomass cannot be effectively utilized – such as materials with high moisture content or significant contaminants that reduce conversion efficiency.
•	Basic Methods of Biomass Utilization: The students were introduced to various pathways for converting biomass into usable energy, including:
o	Direct combustion for heat and power;
o	Thermochemical conversion (pyrolysis, gasification);
o	Biochemical conversion (anaerobic digestion, fermentation);
o	Mechanical extraction (for oils and biofuels).
•	Biomass Power Generation Technologies: A significant portion of the lecture focused on three main combustion approaches:
o	Direct combustion – burning biomass solely as fuel;
o	Mixed combustion – co-firing biomass with coal in existing power plants;
o	Planned combustion – designing dedicated biomass power plants with optimized systems for higher efficiency.
•	Biomass Composition and Reactor Technologies: The lecturer explained the chemical makeup of biomass – primarily cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin – and described how these components behave in thermal processes. Students learned about:
o	Thermogravimetric reactors used to study decomposition behavior;
o	Fluidized bed reactors, which provide excellent heat transfer and mixing for efficient biomass conversion.
•	Biomass Utilization Projects in Jilin and China: The lecturer presented several real-world case studies, including:
o	Four biomass utilization plans and hydrogen parks currently operating in Jilin City;
o	More than 20 similar facilities across China;
o	How these projects contribute to reducing carbon dioxide emissions and support China's Dual Carbon Goals (Carbon Peak 2030, Carbon Neutrality 2060).
•	Production of Methanol and Hydrogen from Biomass: Students learned about the technical routes for extracting methanol gas and hydrogen gas from biomass feedstocks. The lecturer emphasized that hydrogen energy has been elevated to a national strategic level in China's energy policy, with biomass-derived hydrogen offering a low-carbon pathway for the future.
•	Heat Island Effect Mitigation: As an interesting aside, the lecturer also mentioned innovative applications such as special coatings that can reduce the urban heat island effect – linking biomass utilization with broader environmental sustainability.
The session was highly relevant to the students' field of study, bridging fundamental thermodynamics with cutting-edge renewable energy policy and practice. Students asked thoughtful questions about cost competitiveness, feedstock availability, and scalability of biomass technologies.
2. Afternoon Session (2:00 PM) – Chinese Language and Culture Class: "Ancient and Modern Chinese Technology"
The afternoon session was a lively and engaging Chinese language and culture class that traced the evolution of Chinese technological innovation from antiquity to the present day. The class was structured to combine conversational practice, historical knowledge, and grammar exercises.
Conversational Warm-Up
The class began with a friendly discussion in Chinese. Since this was the students' 5th day in China, the teacher invited them to share their impressions of their stay so far – covering topics such as:
•	Food preferences and new dishes they had tried;
•	Entertainment and leisure activities;
•	Shopping experiences;
•	Overall travel and cultural observations.
The students made every effort to respond in Chinese, demonstrating noticeable improvement in their speaking confidence and vocabulary usage.
Overview of Chinese Technological History
The teacher then posed a thought-provoking question: "What technologies do you know that were invented in China?" The timeline stretched from 221 BC (Qin Dynasty) through the Han, Ming, and Yuan dynasties, all the way to modern times – covering a span of almost 2,247 years. Students were then introduced to modern Chinese innovations such as 5G technology, high-speed trains, mobile payments, and space exploration.
The Four Great Inventions of Ancient China
The core of the lesson was dedicated to China's Four Great Inventions, each presented with historical context, global impact, and accompanying language exercises:
1. Papermaking (造纸术)
•	History: The teacher explained how ancient Chinese wrote on bamboo slips (heavy and bulky) and silk (expensive and rare). The invention of Caihou paper (attributed to Cai Lun during the Eastern Han Dynasty) revolutionized documentation. Paper later spread to Japan and eventually to Europe via the Silk Road.
•	Importance: It democratized knowledge and enabled the preservation and dissemination of literature, science, and philosophy.
•	Grammar Practice: Students practiced the sentence structure:
有了——，人们可以——。
Example: 有了纸，人们可以看书。(With paper, people can read books.)
Each student created their own sentences and shared them with the class.
2. Printing (印刷术)
•	History: The teacher traced printing from woodblock printing during the Sui and Tang dynasties to the revolutionary movable type printing invented by Bi Sheng during the Song Dynasty. The evolution continued into modern times, including today's 3D printing technology.
•	Impact: Printing accelerated education, cultural exchange, and the spread of ideas both within China and globally.
•	Grammar Practice: Students practiced:
A和B 都可以——，但A更——。
Example: 我和他都可以说中文，但他的中文更好。(Both he and I can speak Chinese, but his Chinese is better.)
3. Gunpowder (火药)
•	History: The teacher shared the fascinating legend of two Taoist alchemists who accidentally discovered gunpowder over 1,000 years ago while seeking an elixir of immortality. First used during the Sui and Tang dynasties, gunpowder was adopted for military applications in the Song Dynasty. It later spread to the Arab world and then to Europe.
•	Diverse Uses: The teacher emphasized that gunpowder was not solely a weapon – in China, it has also been used in construction, industry, and festive celebrations (such as fireworks).
•	Grammar Practice: Students continued practicing comparative structures using this theme.
4. The Compass (指南针)
•	History: The teacher explained the discovery of lodestone (magnetite) over 2,000 years ago and the creation of the early compass known as "Si Nan" (south-pointing spoon). During the Song Dynasty, the magnetic needle was developed. The compass spread to the Arab world in the 12th century and then to Europe, where it became instrumental in the Age of Discovery.
•	Modern Connection: The teacher linked the ancient compass to modern GPS technology and navigation systems.
•	Grammar Practice: Students practiced:
古代有——，现在有——。它们都可以——。
Example: 古代有指南针，现在有GPS。它们都可以帮我们找方向。(In ancient times there was the compass; now there is GPS. They can both help us find direction.)
Additional Ancient Inventions
Beyond the Four Great Inventions, the teacher highlighted several other remarkable Chinese innovations:
•	Silk – its discovery, production, and role in the Silk Road trade network;
•	Porcelain – its history, craftsmanship, and global influence;
•	The Abacus – for rapid calculation;
•	Astronomy – early star charts and celestial observations;
•	The Seismoscope – Zhang Heng's ancient earthquake detector;
•	The Multiplication Table – used in China long before its adoption elsewhere.
Modern Chinese Inventions and Innovations
To conclude the class, the teacher brought the timeline to the present day, showcasing China's contemporary technological achievements:
•	High-speed rail networks – among the longest and most advanced in the world;
•	5G telecommunications – leading global deployment and standards;

shortReport.description:
1. Morning Session (9:30 AM) – Lecture on "Hydropower Stations and Hydroturbines"
The morning session featured a comprehensive lecture on hydropower technology, delivered by a senior faculty member from NEEPU's School of Energy and Power Engineering. The session was designed to provide students with both fundamental knowledge and practical insights into one of the world's most important renewable energy sources.
The Three Gorges Dam – A National Marvel
The lecture began with a striking visual introduction to the Three Gorges Dam (San Xia) , the world's largest hydropower project. Built in the 1990s on the Yangtze River, the dam generates over 22,500 MW of electricity – accounting for approximately 2% of China's total national power output. The lecturer provided an engaging comparison: this output is equivalent to the energy of ten rocket launch sites, helping students grasp the sheer scale of the project.
Completed in 2003 with its first generator unit coming online in July of that year, the Three Gorges project has since generated over 1.7 trillion kWh of electricity – an amount equivalent to saving 550 million tonnes of standard coal and reducing carbon dioxide emissions by 1.49 billion tonnes. The lecturer emphasized that beyond power generation, the dam serves multiple functions: flood control (having intercepted floods nearly 70 times), navigation improvement (with a cumulative cargo throughput of over 2.1 billion tonnes), and water regulation for the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River.
Learning Objectives
The lecturer outlined three key questions that students should be able to answer by the end of the session:
1.	How does a hydropower station work?
2.	What types of turbines are there?
3.	How is the large amount of electricity stored?
Core Concepts of Hydropower
The lecture systematically addressed these questions:
a) Fundamentals of Hydropower: The lecturer explained the basic principle – converting the potential energy of water at height into kinetic energy as it flows through turbines, which then drives generators to produce electricity. Students were shown images of major waterfalls in China, illustrating the immense natural energy available in flowing water. The lecturer noted that hydropower accounts for a large proportion of China's energy mix, alongside coal, solar, and other renewables.
b) Characteristics and Advantages: Key points included:
•	Hydropower is a renewable energy source derived from the water cycle;
•	Hydropower stations are highly flexible – they can be stopped and started very quickly, making them ideal for load balancing;
•	The structure is less complex compared to thermal power stations;
•	Water storage capacity is crucial for station operation and flood control.
c) Historical Context: The lecturer referenced the 1997 Yangtze River floods, one of the most severe in Chinese history, which underscored the urgent need for large-scale water control infrastructure. This event directly influenced the decision to construct the Three Gorges Dam. The lecturer also mentioned the South-to-North Water Diversion Project (Danjiangkou Reservoir), a massive engineering undertaking designed to redistribute water resources across China.
d) Hydropower Station Types: Students learned about:
•	Diversion hydropower stations, where turbines are installed inside mountains due to limited space around the dam;
•	Pumped storage power stations, which serve as giant batteries – during the day, water flows from reservoirs through turbines to generate electricity, and at night, special pumping machines return the water to higher reservoirs. This technology is particularly important for China, the world's largest electricity producer, which needs to store more energy for grid stability.
e) Turbine Technology – The Heart of the Station: The lecturer provided detailed explanations of:
•	The basic components of water turbines: the runner (or impeller), the snail casing (spiral volute), the rotor, and flow control mechanisms;
•	Different types of water turbines used depending on water head and flow conditions;
•	The Yarlung Zangbo River power station currently under construction, which will be even larger than the Three Gorges Dam.
f) Global Context: The lecturer also noted that the second biggest hydropower station in the world is also located in China, generating 16,000 MW.

Guest Lecture – Uzbekistan's Energy Situation
To conclude the morning session, three PhD graduates from Tashkent State Technical University delivered a brief presentation on Uzbekistan's current energy situation. This segment was particularly relevant, as NEEPU maintains partnership projects with their home institution. The speakers discussed:
•	Uzbekistan's energy mix and reliance on traditional sources;
•	Ongoing renewable energy initiatives;
•	Challenges and opportunities in the country's power sector.
This cross-cultural exchange enriched the lecture by connecting Chinese hydropower technology with the students' home country context.

2. Afternoon Session (2:00 PM) – Chinese Culture Class: "Colorful Traditional Chinese Festivals"
The afternoon session shifted from engineering to cultural studies, focusing on traditional Chinese festivals. The class was designed to combine language practice with cultural immersion.
Conversational Warm-Up
The class began with a friendly discussion in Chinese, encouraging students to share:
•	What traditional festivals they know in both China and Uzbekistan;
•	Whether they had observed any festival-related activities while visiting shopping malls.
New vocabulary introduced included: 传统 (chuántǒng – tradition), 节日 (jiérì – festival), 文化 (wénhuà – culture), and 放假 (fàngjià – holiday). The teacher emphasized that behind every Chinese festival lies a story, making the learning experience both linguistic and narrative-driven.
Overview of Major Chinese Festivals
The teacher presented four major traditional festivals, each illustrated with pictures:
1. Spring Festival (春节) – China's most important holiday, falling on the first day of the first lunar month. The lecturer explained traditions such as family reunions, festive meals, lion dances, and the giving of red envelopes.
2. Qingming Festival (清明节) – Also known as Pure Brightness Day, falling around April 5th. Traditionally a time for offering sacrifices to ancestors, it is also a day for "walking amid greenery" – appreciating spring's arrival.
3. Dragon Boat Festival (端午节) – Held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, this festival honors the memory of the patriotic poet Qu Yuan (c. 340–278 BC), who drowned himself after the fall of the Chu capital. The lecturer explained that people row boats and throw zongzi (rice dumplings wrapped in bamboo leaves) into rivers as offerings. This festival is also celebrated with dragon boat races.
4. Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋节) – Celebrated on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, this festival symbolizes family reunion. The teacher explained the tradition of eating moon cakes and admiring the full moon, a time when families gather together.
Interactive Learning Activities
a) Picture Guessing Game: The teacher showed images associated with each festival and invited students to guess which festival they represented. This activity tested visual recognition and reinforced the cultural symbols of each celebration.
b) Vocabulary Building: Students learned festival-related vocabulary, including:
•	Traditional foods associated with each celebration;
•	Customs and activities unique to each festival.
c) Cross-Cultural Comparison: The teacher asked students to identify similar festivals in Uzbekistan and describe them in Chinese. This exercise encouraged cultural exchange and applied language skills to familiar contexts.
Qu Yuan Poetry Competition
To conclude the class, students were challenged to memorize and recite a verse from Qu Yuan's poetry in front of the entire class. This activity combined cultural appreciation with public speaking practice. The best performers received gifts from the teacher, adding a competitive and rewarding element to the session.
Students were visibly engaged and enthusiastic, with many successfully reciting the verses and demonstrating their language progress over the course of the summer camp.

3. Summary and Reflections
July 2 offered a perfect balance of technical depth and cultural enrichment:
•	The morning hydropower lecture equipped students with a thorough understanding of one of China's most important energy technologies – from the engineering principles of turbines to the strategic significance of pumped storage. The guest lecture on Uzbekistan's energy situation added a personalized dimension to the learning.
•	The afternoon cultural class immersed students in the rich tapestry of Chinese festival traditions, while simultaneously advancing their Mandarin proficiency through vocabulary building, cross-cultural comparison, and performance-based activities.
The combination of engineering and cultural education continues to reflect the summer camp's core mission: preparing students to become globally competent professionals who understand both the technical and human dimensions of energy development.

Excursion to Dream Stars (Changchun) Aerospace Science and Education Museum – July 4, 2026
shortReport.description:
1. Overview of the Museum
On July 4, the student delegation visited the Dream Stars (Changchun) Aerospace Science and Education Museum (筑梦星辰航天科教文旅馆), a state-of-the-art facility located in the Jingyue High-tech Zone of Changchun. The museum, which spans over 6,000 square meters, is built upon Changchun's rich legacy in aerospace and aviation, a city often referred to as a "cradle of aerospace talent".
The museum seamlessly integrates aerospace research, science education, cultural tourism, and interactive entertainment into a comprehensive platform. Using cutting-edge technologies such as naked-eye 3D, virtual reality (VR), and metaverse concepts, the museum brings the mysteries of the universe to life. Its exhibits trace the development of China's space program, from satellite launches and manned spaceflight to lunar and Mars exploration.

2. Thematic Zones and Immersive Exhibits
The museum is divided into two main thematic floors, each dedicated to a different frontier of space exploration.
First Floor – Lunar Exploration Zone
The first floor was centered around lunar exploration. One of the most striking exhibits was the 1:1 scale replica of China's "Tianhe" core module of the Tiangong space station. Students could step inside the module and explore the sleeping quarters, dining area, exercise equipment, and even a water recycling demonstration system, gaining an authentic glimpse into the daily lives of astronauts in orbit.
Another highlight was the "Moon Base" area, which features a highly detailed replica of a lunar rover and a simulation of the lunar surface. The "moon soil" on display was carefully crafted to replicate the composition of real regolith based on data from actual lunar samples. Students could observe models of the Chang'e-4 lander and the Queqiao relay satellite, key components of China's lunar exploration program.
The floor also featured a dedicated China Aerospace History section. Through holographic projection technology, the students were shown the complete timeline of China's space development – from the return of Qian Xuesen to China, to the launch of "Dongfanghong-1" (China's first satellite) in 1970, and through to the major achievements of 2022.
Second Floor – Mars Exploration Zone
The second floor was dedicated to the exploration of Mars, providing students with both scientific knowledge and immersive experiences. Students learned about the planet's ancient environment, including evidence that Mars once had lakes, rivers, and possibly microbial life. The explanation for Mars's distinctive red color was also provided: the planet's surface is rich in iron oxide, which gives it a rusty hue. Furthermore, they learned that 95% of the Martian atmosphere is carbon dioxide – information delivered through interactive exhibits and augmented reality displays.
A key feature on this floor was the replica of the "Zhurong" Mars rover, a meticulously crafted model based on China's actual rover that landed on Mars in 2021. This was complemented by a 3D show that visualized China's Mars exploration missions. Another playful attraction was the "Mars Creature Lab," where a model of a multi-legged alien creature reacted to touch, with glowing eyes and lifelike movements, sparking curiosity about the possibilities of extraterrestrial life.

3. Hands-On Activities and Interactive Simulations
The students actively participated in numerous simulators and interactive experiences throughout both floors.
•	Astronaut Training Simulators: Students tried the "3D Roll Ring" , a device that simulates the multi-axis rotational training astronauts undergo to prepare for the disorienting effects of spaceflight.
•	Rover Control Simulators: The delegation had the chance to control simulated models of lunar and Mars rovers, navigating them across virtual alien terrains.
•	VR and 3D Shows: Students used VR headsets to experience the descent of a return capsule to Earth and explored a 3D animation of a lunar base.
•	Robot Dog Demonstration: A robot dog designed for lunar exploration was showcased, and students had the chance to observe its mobility and functions.

4. Solar System Simulation Hall
A particularly memorable segment was the visit to the Solar System Simulation Hall. Large, textured models of all eight planets were suspended in the hall. Students could touch the planet surfaces, each designed with different materials to simulate the actual composition of the planets.
Adding a sensational dimension to the experience, the museum had set up special spots next to each planet. When students stood on these precise locations, they could hear the "rotation sound" of each planet – audio recordings generated from real satellite data collected from various celestial bodies. This provided an exceptionally immersive and educational encounter.

5. Conclusion
The excursion to the Dream Stars Aerospace Science and Education Museum proved to be an inspiring and highly educational experience. The trip successfully combined knowledge acquisition – covering China's aerospace milestones and planetary science – with interactive fun. The students demonstrated great enthusiasm for the simulators and immersive spaces, deepening their appreciation for China's technological achievements and leaving them with a strong impression of the vast potential of space exploration. The visit concluded with a stop at the souvenir shop, where many students purchased mementos of the experience.
