shortReport.description:
1. Morning Session (9:30 AM) – Lecture on "Introduction to Steam Turbine Power Generation Technology"
The morning session featured a comprehensive lecture on steam turbine power generation technology, delivered by a faculty member from NEEPU's School of Energy and Power Engineering. The session provided students with foundational knowledge about steam turbines, their historical development, structural components, and their critical role in both thermal and nuclear power plants.
What is a Steam Turbine?
The lecturer began by defining the steam turbine as a rotating machinery with steam as the working medium, primarily used as a prime mover for power generation. In thermal power plants, steam turbines drive generators to produce electricity. The lecturer explained that steam turbines also serve as power sources to drive various pumps, fans, and impellers, making them versatile and indispensable in modern industry.
The core principle is straightforward: thermal energy from burning fuel (coal, natural gas, or oil) or from nuclear fission is used to generate high-pressure steam, which then expands through the turbine, converting thermal energy into mechanical energy. This mechanical energy is then transformed into electrical energy by a generator. The lecturer emphasized that in both thermal and nuclear power plants, the turbine is the key component that drives the generator – the difference lies only in the heat source.
The lecturer also clarified that burning coal involves an oxidation process, while nuclear power relies on fission reactions, but both ultimately produce steam to drive the turbine.
Historical Development of Steam Turbines
The lecturer presented a fascinating historical overview, tracing the evolution of steam turbine technology:
•	1883 – The Birth of the First Axial-Flow Steam Turbine: Swedish engineer Laval built the first axial-flow steam turbine with a power output of 5 horsepower (approximately 3.7 kW). Laval also pioneered the development of nozzles to accelerate steam flow, a fundamental innovation still used today .
•	1884–1894 – The Reaction Turbine: British engineer Parsons developed the first reaction steam turbine with an output of 10 horsepower, later scaled to 100 kW .
•	1900 – The Curtis Turbine: American engineer Curtis built the first multi-stage impulse turbine, introducing the concept of velocity compounding.
•	1900–1903 – Multi-Stage Impulse Turbines: French engineer Rateau and Swiss engineer Zoelly independently developed multi-stage impulse turbines.
•	1920 – Feedwater Regenerative Steam Turbine: Regenerative feedwater heating was introduced, significantly improving cycle efficiency.
•	1925 – Intermediate Reheat Steam Turbine: Reheating between turbine stages was introduced to increase efficiency and reduce moisture in the low-pressure stages.
•	1930 – Radial Flow Turbine: Siemens of Germany developed a radial flow turbine design.
•	1937 – Soviet Union's 100 MW Unit: The Leningrad Metal Factory produced a 100 MW steam turbine.
The lecturer noted that after World War II, economic recovery drove a surge in electricity demand, leading to continuous increases in unit capacity. By the 1960s, 1000 MW turbines were manufactured, and in the 1970s, 1300 MW units were produced.
Development of Steam Turbines in China
The lecturer provided a detailed account of China's steam turbine development:
•	1955 – Shanghai Turbine Factory produced China's first 6000 kW turbine, installed at Tianjia'an Power Plant in Huainan.
•	1958–1959 – Shanghai and Harbin Turbine Factories produced 50 MW and 100 MW units.
•	1960 – Harbin Turbine Factory began developing 200 MW units, commissioned in 1972 at Chaoyang.
•	1974 – Shanghai Turbine Factory produced a 300 MW unit for Zouxian Power Plant.
•	Ten years later – Harbin Turbine Factory produced a 600 MW unit for Pingwei Power Plant.
•	2001 – Harbin and Shanghai Turbine Factories produced 650 MW nuclear steam turbines.
Today, China commonly uses 600–1000 MW units for base-load power generation, along with 300 MW units for heating applications. The lecturer also noted that China initially adopted Soviet and Japanese turbine technology before developing its own indigenous capabilities.
Major Manufacturers
The lecturer introduced the world's leading steam turbine manufacturers:
•	GE (General Electric, USA) – impulse type turbines;
•	Westinghouse (USA) – reaction type turbines;
•	BBC (Brown Boveri, Switzerland) – reaction type turbines;
•	Alstom (France) – both impulse and reaction types;
•	Other manufacturers – including Soviet/Leningrad and Japanese/Toshiba.
In China, the "Big Three" power equipment factories are:
•	Harbin Turbine Factory
•	Shanghai Turbine Factory
•	Dongfang Turbine Factory
Medium and small-sized turbine factories include Beijing Heavy Motor, Qingdao Turbine, and Wuhan Turbine. For industrial steam turbines, the leading manufacturer is Hangzhou Steam Turbine Factory, while Nanjing Turbine Factory specializes in gas turbines.
The lecturer also mentioned that Datang in Uzbekistan is currently constructing a thermal power plant that will generate 600–1000 MW of power. The typical lifespan of a thermal power plant is around 30 years, after which equipment is replaced or upgraded.
Structure of a Steam Turbine
The lecturer provided a detailed explanation of the turbine's main components:
a) The Stage: The fundamental working unit of a turbine, consisting of a stationary nozzle cascade (stator) and a rotating blade cascade (rotor). Steam expands through the nozzles, accelerating and directing it onto the rotor blades, where it imparts rotational force.
b) The Rotor: The rotating part of the turbine, responsible for energy conversion and torque transmission. Rotors can be classified as:
•	Wheel-type – typically used in impulse turbines;
•	Drum-type – typically used in reaction turbines.
Wheel-type rotors come in four structural forms: integral (monobloc), assembled, welded, and combined rotors. The lecturer showed images of each type, explaining their respective advantages.
c) Cylinder (Casing): The stationary outer shell of the turbine, which contains the pressure and temperature of the steam. Cylinders can be:
•	Single-layer, double-layer, or triple-layer – with multi-layer designs offering better thermal stress management.
The lecturer explained that high and medium-pressure cylinders operate at very high temperatures and pressures, requiring thick walls and large flanges. Low-pressure cylinders, while operating at lower temperatures, are much larger in size due to the increased steam volume at low pressure – especially in the exhaust section.
d) Diaphragms and Diaphragm Sleeves: These form the inter-stage walls, fixing the stationary blades and preventing steam leakage between stages. They are divided into welded diaphragms (offering higher strength and better sealing) and cast diaphragms.
e) Bearings: Steam turbines use two types of bearings:
•	Radial support bearings – to support the rotor's weight, maintain radial position, and ensure correct clearances;
•	Thrust bearings – to absorb axial thrust and maintain the rotor's axial position.
f) Couplings: These connect different sections of the rotor and the generator. There are three main types:
•	Rigid coupling – fully transmits force and displacement (used between turbine sections);
•	Semi-flexible coupling – absorbs some force and displacement (used between turbine and generator);
•	Flexible coupling – transmits no axial thrust and little vibration (now rarely used).
Practical Significance
The lecturer emphasized that steam turbines generate more than 60% of the world's electricity (including both thermal and nuclear power), making them absolutely vital to the global economy. The presentation also included a short video and maintenance site photos to give students a real-world perspective on turbine construction and servicing.

2. Afternoon Session (2:00 PM) – Chinese Culture Class: "Beautiful Traditional Chinese Clothing"
The afternoon session was a vibrant exploration of traditional Chinese clothing, combining cultural history, vocabulary building, and interactive discussion. The teacher noticed that a few students had come to class wearing qipao and warmly complimented them, creating an immediate sense of connection to the topic.
Opening Discussion: Traditional Clothing of Uzbekistan
The teacher began by inviting students to share the names of their traditional Uzbek garments in Chinese. Students contributed the following vocabulary:
•	长袍 (chángpáo) – long robe/coat, often quilted or made of silk;
•	袷袢 (qiāpàn) – the classic Uzbek men's striped silk robe, worn over a shirt;
•	绣花小圆帽 (xiùhuā xiǎo yuán mào) – embroidered round skullcap (men's);
•	头巾 (tóujīn) – headscarf (women's, often brightly colored);
•	艾德莱斯绸裙 (Àidéláisī chóu qún) – adras/ikat silk dress, a very iconic women's garment;
•	灯笼裤 (dēnglongkù) – wide, tapered harem pants worn by both genders under robes.
The teacher expressed surprise and delight upon learning that 130 nationalities live in Uzbekistan, with 114 of them residing in Samarkand – a testament to the country's extraordinary cultural diversity. She encouraged students to write the Chinese names of their traditional clothing on the board, which they did with enthusiasm.
Introduction to Hanfu and Chinese Clothing
The teacher introduced key vocabulary: 衣服 (yīfu – clothing), 传统 (chuántǒng – tradition), 漂亮 (piàoliang – beautiful), 汉服 (hànfú – Han clothing), and 旗袍 (qípáo – cheongsam).
The teacher explained that China has 56 officially recognized ethnic groups, each with its own traditional clothing. The Han ethnic group is the majority (over 91% of the population), so the primary traditional clothing is Hanfu – flowing robes with crossed collars and wide sleeves, worn for over 3,000 years.
A video was shown illustrating the evolution of Hanfu across different dynasties, highlighting that the Tang Dynasty (618–907 AD) featured particularly diverse and elaborate styles. Students observed that clothing in the Yuan and Qing dynasties is not called Hanfu, as those periods were ruled by Mongol and Manchu dynasties, not the Han ethnic group.
Key Features of Hanfu
The teacher pointed out distinctive features of Hanfu, such as the wide, flowing sleeves that resemble fans. A new grammatical structure was introduced: 像…一样 (xiàng… yīyàng – "like… just as"). Students practiced constructing sentences such as: 袖子像扇子一样 (The sleeves are like fans). Volunteers came to the front to create their own sentences using this structure.
The teacher also introduced the philosophical concept of 天人合一 (tiān rén hé yī – "unity of heaven and humanity") , explaining how this deeply rooted Chinese belief is reflected in traditional clothing design – with garments symbolizing harmony between humans and nature. Another key phrase was 礼仪之邦 (lǐyí zhī bāng – "a nation of etiquette") , emphasizing that traditional clothing in China is closely linked to social manners and ritual propriety. The teacher also taught the word 审美 (shěnměi – aesthetic appreciation) , noting that 每个人的审美不一样 (everyone's aesthetic is different).
A second video demonstrated the correct way to put on Hanfu, showing the proper sequence and tying techniques – information that fascinated the students, as they had not realized the process was so structured.
Qipao and Modern Chinese Clothing
The teacher then introduced the qipao (cheongsam) , a high-collared, body-hugging gown that originated during the Qing Dynasty and later evolved into the modern version seen today. The teacher noted that there are many different types of qipao in different regions of China. Students learned the word 扣子 (kòuzi – buttons) , but specifically for qipao, they are called 盘扣 (pánkòu) – a straight-shaped knot button that is an integral part of the qipao's aesthetic.
The Chinese Tunic Suit (中山装)
The teacher also discussed the 中山装 (Zhōngshān zhuāng – Chinese tunic suit) , named after Sun Yat-sen, who influenced its design. The teacher introduced the phrase 礼义廉耻 (lǐ yì lián chǐ – "propriety, righteousness, honesty, and a sense of shame") , and challenged students to memorize these four characters. Students were then called upon randomly to write them on the board by heart – a fun and competitive activity that showcased their character recognition skills.
Diversity of Ethnic Clothing
A final video was shown, featuring the traditional clothing of China's 56 ethnic groups – from the elaborate silver ornaments of the Miao to the colorful embroidered garments of the Yi. The teacher introduced additional vocabulary: 时尚 (shíshàng – fashionable) and 流行 (liúxíng – popular/trendy) , noting that traditional Chinese clothing has become both fashionable and popular among young people in modern China.
The teacher mentioned that if students travel to larger cities like Xi'an, Beijing, or Shanghai, they will see many young people wearing modern Chinese traditional clothing as part of their daily fashion, not just during festivals – a testament to the ongoing revival of Hanfu culture.
3. Summary and Reflections
July 6 was another day of perfect balance between technical education and cultural immersion:
•	The morning steam turbine lecture provided students with a solid technical foundation in one of the most important machines in power generation. From Laval's first 5-horsepower turbine to today's 1000 MW giants, students traced the remarkable journey of this technology, while also learning about its structure, components, and manufacturers.
•	The afternoon clothing culture class immersed students in the rich visual and philosophical world of Chinese traditional attire – from Hanfu's flowing elegance to the qipao's modern sophistication, and from the diversity of 56 ethnic groups to the cultural significance of Sun Yat-sen's tunic suit.
The students left both sessions with expanded knowledge, practical language skills, and a deeper appreciation for both the engineering and cultural dimensions of China.

1. Morning Session (9:30 AM) – Lecture on "Overview of the Development of Refrigeration and Heat Pump Technology"
The morning session featured a comprehensive lecture delivered by Professor Liu Zhongyan from NEEPU's School of Energy and Power Engineering. The session provided students with a broad understanding of refrigeration and heat pump technologies, their historical development, working principles, environmental challenges, and future directions.
Refrigeration in Daily Life and Industry
The lecturer began by showing pictures of everyday household equipment – refrigerators, freezers, and air conditioners – to help students recognize the refrigeration technology that surrounds them. The scope quickly expanded to include large-scale applications:
•	Cold storage and the cold chain: The lecturer traced the roadmap of perishable products from factories to customers, highlighting refrigerated warehouses,冷链 vehicles, transit warehouses, and retail display cases.
•	The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics: Many events relied heavily on refrigeration technology – from the "Snow Ruyi" ski jumping venue to the "Ice Cube" curling venue, the "Ice Ribbon" speed skating oval, and the figure skating rink at Capital Gymnasium.
•	Museums and cultural heritage: Refrigeration systems maintain stable temperature and humidity for preserving artifacts.
•	Industrial applications: Semiconductor manufacturing requires ultra-stable temperatures for wafer and chip production.
•	Scientific research and aerospace: Refrigeration creates low-temperature environments for experiments and simulates space conditions.
The lecturer emphasized that refrigeration spans from aerospace to daily life – it is deeply integrated into human civilization.
Definition and Classification of Refrigeration
Refrigeration was defined as the process of lowering and maintaining the temperature of an object or space below that of its surroundings.
Natural cold resources include:
•	Natural ice and snow
•	Deep well water
•	Underground soil (cold storage)
•	Outdoor air in winter
Artificial cold resources are created through physical, chemical, or biological methods, such as:
•	Electric refrigeration machines
•	Absorption refrigerators
•	Evaporative cooling
•	Winter outdoor air utilization
Refrigeration is classified by temperature range:
•	Ordinary refrigeration: Above -120°C – used in air conditioning, food storage, and industrial cooling.
•	Deep refrigeration: 20 K (-253.15°C) to -120°C – used in air separation, LNG manufacturing, and chemical processes.
•	Ultra-low temperature: 0.3 K to 20 K – used in superconductivity and space environment simulation.
Historical Development of Refrigeration Technology
The lecturer traced refrigeration history from ancient times to the modern era:
Natural Cold Era:
•	Ancient Chinese used ice cellars as early as the Zhou Dynasty. The Qing Huidian (清会典) recorded that in 1644, the Ministry of Works would collect ice for the Forbidden City, with one ice cellar storing 4,543 blocks.
•	A remarkable bronze "Jianfou" (ice chest) from the Warring States period (excavated in 1978 from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng in Suizhou, Hubei) had a double-layer structure – the outer layer held ice, the inner layer held food and drinks.
•	Ice harvesting on the Hudson River in America was a major 19th-century industry.
Artificial Cold Era – Key Milestones:
•	1755: Scottish chemist William Cullen used ether evaporation to freeze water.
•	1834: American inventor Jacob Perkins built the first vapor-compression refrigeration machine using ether.
•	1859: French engineer Ferdinand Carré invented the ammonia-water absorption refrigeration system.
•	1875: German engineer Carl von Linde invented the ammonia vapor-compression refrigerator – the prestigious Linde Award in international refrigeration is named after him.
The Air Conditioning Revolution:
•	1902: Willis Carrier designed the first modern air conditioning system for a Brooklyn printing plant. He later published the psychrometric chart in 1911, founded the Carrier Corporation in 1915, and developed centrifugal chillers in 1922 and automotive AC in 1939. He is revered as the "Father of Air Conditioning" and was named by Time magazine as one of the 100 most influential people of the 20th century.
The Fluorocarbon Era:
•	1928: Thomas Midgley Jr. synthesized R12 (CFC-12) , a non-toxic, non-flammable refrigerant that revolutionized the industry. He also invented tetraethyl lead as a gasoline additive. He was later dubbed "the single organism that has had the greatest impact on Earth's atmosphere" – both for his contributions and their unintended consequences.
Common Refrigeration Methods
The lecturer systematically presented various refrigeration methods based on physical principles:
1. Vapor-Compression Refrigeration
The most widely used method, based on the phase change (liquid-to-vapor) principle. When a liquid evaporates, it absorbs latent heat – for example, water's latent heat of vaporization at 100°C is 2,256.9 kJ/kg, and at 5°C it is 2,489.8 kJ/kg. The system uses a compressor to continuously remove vapor and a condenser to return the refrigerant to liquid state.
2. Absorption Refrigeration
Driven by thermal energy (heat) rather than mechanical work. The system uses an absorber, generator, and solution pump along with evaporator, condenser, and expansion valve. It is often used in waste heat recovery applications.
3. Adsorption Refrigeration
Uses solid adsorbents (such as zeolites) that adsorb and desorb refrigerant gases in response to temperature changes. During daytime, heating drives desorption; at night, cooling enables adsorption and evaporation, creating a refrigeration effect.
4. Gas Expansion Refrigeration
High-pressure gas expands adiabatically through a throttle valve or expander, reducing temperature. Used in aircraft air conditioning systems and cryogenic applications.
5. Thermoelectric (Peltier) Cooling
Based on the Peltier effect (discovered in 1834) – an electric current creates a temperature difference. Used in infrared detectors, spacecraft (including Hubble Space Telescope), and precision instruments. Advantages: no moving parts; disadvantages: low efficiency and high cost.
6. Evaporative Cooling
Uses water evaporation to cool air. Direct evaporative cooling cools air directly; indirect evaporative cooling produces chilled water. Widely used in data centers and dry climates.
7. Sky Radiation Cooling
On clear nights, terrestrial surfaces radiate heat to the cold sky. Cooling rates can reach 75 W/m². A new radiative cooling metamaterial (SiO₂ microspheres embedded in polymethylpentene film) was invented by Professor Yang Ronggui of the University of Colorado.
Refrigerants and Environmental Challenges
The lecturer devoted significant attention to the environmental impact of refrigerants:
•	CFCs (Chlorofluorocarbons): Thomas Midgley's invention in 1928, later found to destroy the ozone layer.
•	1974: Professors M.J. Molina and F.S. Rowland of the University of California published their landmark paper linking CFCs to ozone depletion. A single chlorine atom can destroy 10³–10⁴ ozone molecules.
•	1995: Molina, Rowland, and Dutch scientist Paul Crutzen received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on stratospheric ozone chemistry.
Key international agreements:
•	1992: Montreal Protocol – phased out CFCs and later HCFCs.
•	1997: Kyoto Protocol – addressed greenhouse gas emissions.
•	2009: Copenhagen Accord.
•	2015: Paris Agreement – aiming to limit global temperature rise to 2°C (preferably 1.5°C).
•	2016: Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol – targets the phase-down of HFCs (high-GWP refrigerants like R134a, R410A, R407C, R404A), potentially contributing to 0.5°C of warming avoidance by 2100.
•	China completely phased out CFCs and halons by 2007 – two and a half years ahead of the Montreal Protocol schedule.
Heat Pump Technology
The lecturer introduced the heat pump by analogy with a water pump – just as a pump moves water uphill, a heat pump moves heat from a low-temperature source to a high-temperature sink, using external energy (usually electricity).
Key definitions:
•	A heat pump is a device that, driven by high-grade energy, forces heat from a low-temperature source to a high-temperature sink.
•	It supplies useful heat that is the sum of the input work and the extracted heat, making it highly energy-efficient.
Types of heat pumps:
•	Air-source heat pumps
•	Ground-source (geothermal) heat pumps
•	Water-source heat pumps (groundwater, surface water, seawater)
Historical milestones:
•	1927: British engineer Haldane installed the first domestic heat pump in Scotland.
•	1930–1931: The first large-capacity heat pump (1050 kW, COP 2.5) was installed in Los Angeles.
•	1938–1939: The first European large heat pump (175 kW) was installed in Zurich, supplying 60°C water to a municipal hall.
•	1984–1992: Japan's "Super Heat Pump" project achieved COP up to 4.5 for cooling/heating, 6 for hot water (85°C), and 2.3 for industrial heating (150–300°C).
Refrigeration and Heat Pump Equipment
The lecturer showcased various modern equipment types:
•	Heat pump water heaters – extracting heat from air to produce hot water, with CO₂ as a natural refrigerant (ODP=0, GWP=1) in transcritical cycles.
•	Absorption heat exchangers – acting like "temperature transformers" that allow heat transfer between flows with mismatched heat capacities. Type I reduces temperature differences; Type II amplifies them – widely used in district heating and waste heat recovery.
•	Maglev centrifugal chillers – featuring magnetic bearings, variable speed, direct drive, and two-stage compression. Advantages: oil-free, simple design, lightweight, excellent part-load performance.
•	Dual-mode ice storage units – used for both air conditioning and ice making (evaporator temperatures below -6°C).
•	Room air conditioners – available in monobloc, split, fixed-speed, and inverter (variable-speed) types.
•	Multi-split systems (VRF/VRV) – large-capacity inverter air conditioners with multiple indoor units.
•	Water-source heat pumps – used in ground-source heat pump systems with reversing water valves for heating/cooling switching.
•	Household air-source heat pump/chiller units – one machine for both cooling and heating, playing a significant role in northern China's "coal-to-clean-energy" heating transition.
•	Terminal equipment – fan coil units (cooling/heating), radiant floor heating (comfortable), radiators (require higher water temperatures).

2. Afternoon Session (2:00 PM) – Chinese Culture Class: "The Chinese 'Nian' Holiday – Spring Festival"
The afternoon session was a vibrant cultural class introducing students to China's most important traditional festival – the Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) . The teacher began with a famous quote from the Song Dynasty poet Su Shi (苏轼) : "此心安处是吾乡" (Home is where the heart finds peace) , setting a warm and welcoming tone.
The Legend of the Nian Beast
The teacher recounted the ancient legend of "Nian" (年) , a mythical beast that would descend from the mountains on New Year's Eve to harm people and livestock. The villagers discovered that Nian feared three things: the color red, firelight, and loud noises. Thus began the traditions of pasting red papers, lighting fires, and setting off firecrackers – all to pray for blessings and ward off disasters.
The Long History of Spring Festival
The teacher explained that the Spring Festival has over 4,000 years of history, dating back to the Shang Dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC) , when it originated as sacrificial ceremonies. During the Han Dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) , the first day of the first lunar month was officially established as New Year's Day. The festival was formalized as a statutory holiday in modern China.
In 2023, the Spring Festival became a UN Floating Holiday, and in 2024, it was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Today, nearly 20 countries around the world celebrate the Spring Festival.
A Continuous Celebration Cycle
The teacher emphasized that Spring Festival is not a single day but a continuous celebration cycle lasting about 20 days, from Little Year (腊月二十三) to the Lantern Festival (正月十五) :
1. Little Year (小年) – The Prelude
•	Date: The 23rd day of the 12th lunar month.
•	Customs: Sending the Kitchen God to report to heaven; spring cleaning to sweep away bad luck; preparing New Year goods (candy, offerings).
2. New Year's Eve (除夕) – The Climax Eve
•	The last day of the lunar year.
•	Customs: Family reunion dinner (年夜饭); staying up late (守岁); pasting spring couplets (春联); honoring ancestors (祭祖).
3. Spring Festival (春节) – The First Day
•	The first day of the new lunar year.
•	Customs: Opening firecrackers (开门爆竹); paying New Year visits (拜年); giving red envelopes with money (压岁钱) to children.
4. Lantern Festival (元宵节) – The Finale
•	The 15th day of the first lunar month.
•	Customs: Watching lantern displays, eating yuanxiao (sweet rice dumplings), and enjoying festive parades.
Colorful Customs and Traditions
The teacher vividly described the rich customs associated with the festival:
Preparations:
•	Shopping (买年货): Buying food, clothes, and necessities.
•	Cleaning (大扫除): Thorough house cleaning to sweep away the bad luck of the old year.
•	Pasting "Fu" and Couplets: "福" (blessing) is pasted upside down, symbolizing "福到了" (blessing has arrived) . The color red symbolizes good luck and joy.
New Year's Eve:
•	Making Dumplings (包饺子): Whole families make dumplings together. Dumplings are shaped like ancient gold ingots (元宝), symbolizing wealth. Some families hide a coin inside – the lucky finder will have good fortune in the coming year.
•	Reunion Dinner (年夜饭): The most important meal of the year. Dishes carry symbolic meanings:
o	Fish (鱼) – "年年有余" (surplus every year)
o	Rice cake (年糕) – "步步高升" (advance step by step)
o	Dumplings (饺子) – "招财进宝" (attract wealth)
o	Tangyuan (汤圆) – "团团圆圆" (family reunion)
•	Fireworks and Staying Up Late: Fireworks bid farewell to the old and welcome the new; staying up late (守岁) ensures longevity for parents.
New Year's Day and Beyond:
•	Wearing New Clothes: 穿新衣，戴新帽，新年新气象 (new clothes, new hat – new year, new look).
•	New Year Visits (拜年): People visit family, friends, and neighbors, exchanging greetings and good wishes.
New Year Greetings
The teacher taught students essential Spring Festival greetings:
Chinese	Pinyin	English
过年好！	Guò Nián Hǎo	Happy New Year!
新年快乐！	Xīn Nián Kuài Lè	Happy New Year!
恭喜发财！	Gōng Xǐ Fā Cái	Wish you wealth!
万事如意！	Wàn Shì Rú Yì	May everything go well!
身体健康！	Shēn Tǐ Jiàn Kāng	Good health!
Students came to the board in pairs to practice these phrases with each other. The best performers received small gifts from the teacher.
The Spirit of Spring Festival
The teacher emphasized that Spring Festival is far more than a holiday – it embodies the core values of Chinese civilization:
•	团圆 (Reunion): Family is everything. No matter how far, people go home.
•	感恩 (Gratitude): Thankfulness for the past year's harvest and blessings.
•	希望 (Hope): New beginnings, new dreams.
•	狂欢 (Celebration): Welcoming new life with the warmest joy.
The World's Biggest Festival
The teacher shared astonishing statistics:
•	4 billion trips during 春运 (Chunyun) – the world's largest annual human migration.
•	3 billion people watch the Spring Festival Gala – the most-watched TV program globally.
•	15 days of nationwide celebration – from New Year's Eve to the Lantern Festival.
The teacher also introduced other festive cultural activities:
•	Dragon dances (舞龙)
•	Yingge dance (英歌舞) – a form of Chinese folk dance
•	Walking on stilts (踩高跷)
•	Temple fairs (庙会)
3. Summary and Reflections
July 7 offered a remarkable duality of technical and cultural learning:
•	The morning refrigeration and heat pump lecture provided students with a comprehensive understanding of the historical development, scientific principles, environmental challenges, and cutting-edge technologies in this vital field. From ancient ice cellars to maglev compressors and the Kigali Amendment, students traced the full arc of refrigeration's evolution and its critical role in modern civilization.
•	The afternoon Spring Festival class immersed students in the warmth, color, and depth of China's most important traditional celebration. From the legend of the Nian beast to UNESCO recognition, from dumpling-making to Spring Festival greetings, students gained not only vocabulary but also a deep appreciation for the cultural spirit of reunion, gratitude, hope, and celebration.
The students left both sessions with expanded knowledge, practical language skills, and a greater appreciation for both the engineering and humanistic dimensions of Chinese culture.

1. Morning Excursion – Jilin Beishan Four Seasons Cross-Country Ski Resort (9:00 AM)
On the morning of July 8, the delegation visited the Jilin Beishan Four Seasons Cross-Country Ski Resort, a world-class facility that provided a striking contrast to the summer heat outside.
A Marvel of Engineering and Sports
The ski resort is located within the Jilin Beishan Scenic Area. It is renowned as the world's first indoor cross-country ski resort rebuilt and expanded from a civil air defense project, the first of its kind in Asia, and the fourth in the world (after Finland, Sweden, and Germany). With its complete facilities and international standards, it serves as a key training base for China's national ski teams .
Key Features and Facilities
The resort covers a total construction area of 25,244 square meters. Key features include :
•	Indoor Snow Track: 1,308 meters long, 8 meters wide, with a slope of 8°, and a constant indoor temperature of approximately -6°C all year round .
•	Outdoor Snow Track: 1.6 kilometers long, 4 meters wide, with a slope of 14° .
•	Departure Hall: About 3,000 square meters, connecting the indoor and outdoor tracks .
•	Other Facilities: Includes a shooting range, penalty loop, and viewing trails for public use .
A "Snow Cave" in Summer
Stepping from the summer heat into the -6°C indoor environment was a dramatic experience. The perfectly maintained snow track and the 100-meter Rime Corridor were highlights. The rime, which mimics the famous winter scenery of Jilin, is the country's only indoor rime laboratory .
•	Professional Training: The resort provides year-round, all-weather training for national teams in cross-country skiing, Nordic combined, and biathlon, significantly saving costs compared to overseas training .
•	Public Experience: For the students, it offered a rare opportunity to feel the thrill of winter sports in the middle of summer.

The visit to the Jilin Beishan Four Seasons Cross-Country Ski Resort was not merely a recreational outing – it was a living demonstration of the refrigeration principles the students had learned just one day earlier. As they stepped from the summer heat into the -6°C indoor environment, they witnessed firsthand how the theories from Professor Liu's lecture are applied in large-scale, real-world engineering.
1. Large-Scale Refrigeration Systems – Beyond Household Appliances
During the July 7 lecture, the students learned that refrigeration spans "from aerospace to daily life." The ski resort exemplifies this on an industrial scale:
•	Continuous Cooling Demand: Unlike a household refrigerator that maintains a small enclosed space, the ski resort must continuously cool over 25,000 square meters of indoor space with a 1,308-meter-long snow track – 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. This requires massive industrial-grade vapor-compression refrigeration systems, the same principle as the household units but scaled up exponentially.
•	Load Calculation: The students could appreciate the immense cooling load involved. Maintaining -6°C when outdoor summer temperatures in Jilin often exceed 30°C requires:
o	A high-capacity refrigeration plant (likely using ammonia or CO₂ as a refrigerant, both mentioned in the lecture as natural alternatives with zero ODP);
o	Powerful compressors and condensers to reject heat to the outside air;
o	Extensive insulation to minimize heat gain from the surrounding ground and atmosphere.
2. The Refrigerant Dilemma – Theory Applied
The July 7 lecture devoted significant time to refrigerants and their environmental impact – from CFCs and HCFCs to the Montreal Protocol, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, and the Kigali Amendment. At the ski resort, the choice of refrigerant is a critical engineering decision:
•	The facility must use a refrigerant that is efficient at low evaporating temperatures (below -6°C) while complying with Chinese and international environmental regulations.
•	The students could reflect on whether the resort uses synthetic refrigerants (like HFCs, which have high GWP and are being phased down) or natural refrigerants (like ammonia (NH₃) or CO₂, which have ODP=0 and very low GWP).
•	This real-world application brings to life the challenges the lecturer described: balancing performance, safety, cost, and environmental responsibility.
3. Heat Pump Principles in Reverse – The Ski Resort as a "Heat Source"
The July 7 lecture introduced the heat pump as a device that moves heat from a low-temperature source to a high-temperature sink. The ski resort essentially operates as a giant refrigeration system – but the rejected heat (the "waste heat" from the condensers) is not necessarily wasted:
•	The students might have noticed that the resort has a departure hall, viewing platforms, and other public areas that need heating in winter.
•	In principle, the condenser heat from the refrigeration system could be captured and used for space heating, domestic hot water, or even melting snow on walkways – effectively making the resort a combined cooling and heating system.
•	This is a direct parallel to the heat recovery systems and absorption heat exchangers discussed in the lecture – turning a "waste" output into a useful resource.
4. Evaporative Cooling and Thermal Storage – Advanced Concepts at Work
The resort's indoor rime corridor (100 meters of artificial frost-covered trees) offers another connection:
•	The rime is produced by evaporative cooling – spraying water droplets into the cold air, where they freeze upon contact. This is the same principle as the sky radiation cooling and evaporative cooling methods discussed in the lecture, but applied on a micro-scale for aesthetic effect.
•	The resort likely uses thermal energy storage – either as chilled water or ice – to shift cooling loads to off-peak hours when electricity is cheaper. This parallels the dual-mode ice storage cooling units described in the lecture, which produce ice at night for use during daytime peak hours.
5. System Efficiency – The Imperative of COP
The lecture emphasized the Coefficient of Performance (COP) as a measure of refrigeration system efficiency. At the ski resort, efficiency is paramount:
•	A large-scale facility like this consumes enormous amounts of electricity. Any inefficiency directly translates to higher operating costs and greater environmental impact.
•	The students could observe that the resort likely uses:
o	Variable-speed compressors (inverter technology) to match cooling output to demand – just like the "变频空调器" (inverter air conditioners) mentioned in the lecture;
o	High-efficiency heat exchangers to maximize heat transfer;
o	Advanced control systems to optimize the entire refrigeration cycle.
6. The "Frozen" Paradox – Why This Technology Matters
The lecturer on July 7 noted that refrigeration is "very closely related to human daily life." The ski resort exemplifies this in a unique way:
•	It allows winter sports to be enjoyed year-round, promoting health and recreation.
•	It provides a training ground for athletes without requiring expensive overseas travel.
•	It demonstrates how engineering can overcome natural limitations – creating a microclimate that defies the seasons.
For the students, stepping from 30°C summer heat into a -6°C "snow cave" was not just a thrill – it was a tangible experience of the power of refrigeration technology. The comfortable, controlled environment they enjoyed was the result of the very principles they had studied: vapor compression, phase change, heat rejection, insulation, and system optimization.

The Beishan Ski Resort visit transformed the abstract concepts of the July 7 lecture into a tangible, dynamic reality. The students could:
•	See the results of large-scale refrigeration (snow in summer);
•	Feel the effect of continuous cooling (a stable -6°C environment);
•	Understand the engineering challenges (maintaining that environment against external heat gain);
•	Connect the technologies to environmental and economic considerations (refrigerant choice, energy efficiency).
This excursion vividly demonstrated that refrigeration technology is not confined to classrooms or household appliances – it is a foundational engineering discipline that enables modern life, from food preservation and comfortable buildings to international sports and scientific research. The visit to Beishan was, in essence, a three-dimensional field laboratory for the principles learned on July 7.

2. Afternoon Excursion – Longtan Mountain Park (2:30 PM)
In the afternoon, the group visited Longtan Mountain Park, one of Jilin City's "Four Famous Mountains," known for its rich history and natural beauty. Entry to the park is free .
A Natural and Historical Gem
Longtan Mountain, formerly known as Nishha Mountain, is a branch of the Changbai Mountain range. The park is a harmonious blend of natural scenery, ancient temples, and historical relics, making it a national forest park .
Historical Significance
The mountain is home to the Longtan Mountain City, an ancient military fortress built during the Goguryeo period (circa 410 AD). The city walls, built along the mountain ridges, stretch for 2,396 meters .
Major Sites Visited
•	The "Water Prison" (Longtan): An ancient reservoir built during the Goguryeo period, located in the northwest corner of the mountain city. It measures 52.8 meters long and 25.75 meters wide, with a depth of over 9 meters. According to legend, it is also the home of a dragon, giving the mountain its name. The "Longtan Yinyue" (Moon over the Dragon Pool) is one of the "Eight Scenic Views of Jilin" .
•	The "Dry Prison": A circular stone pit, about 10.6 meters in diameter and 2-3 meters deep, believed to have been used as a military granary or storage cellar .
•	Nan Tian Men (South Heavenly Gate): The highest peak of the mountain at 388.3 meters. From the viewing platform here, the students could enjoy a breathtaking panorama of Jilin City and the winding Songhua River .
•	Longfeng Temple: A collection of ancient temples including the Dragon King Temple, Guanyin Hall, and Guan Yu Temple. Historical records show that the Qianlong Emperor visited and inscribed a plaque during his Eastern Inspection tour in 1754 .

3. Summary and Reflections
The excursions on July 8 offered a perfect balance of modern sporting achievement and ancient cultural heritage.
•	The Beishan Four Seasons Ski Resort showcased China's engineering capabilities and its commitment to winter sports, offering the students a novel and refreshing experience.
•	The Longtan Mountain Park excursion provided a journey through history, where students could explore the legacy of ancient kingdoms and appreciate the profound cultural layers of the region.
These visits were a valuable complement to the students' academic program, enriching their understanding of China's diverse landscape and civilization.

9:30 Morning Session – Lecture on "Modern Energy Storage Technologies and Their Development Trends"
The morning session provided students with a comprehensive overview of energy storage technologies, their necessity, working principles, and future development trends. The lecture systematically addressed three core questions: Why do we need energy storage? What are the key technologies? And where are they applied?
Why Energy Storage is Essential
The lecturer began by explaining the fundamental challenge facing modern power systems. Unlike traditional power generation that can be dispatched on demand, renewable energy sources like solar and wind power rely entirely on natural conditions – sunshine and wind availability fluctuate throughout the day and across seasons. This intermittency creates a mismatch between generation and consumption.
The concept of "Source-Grid-Load-Storage" synergy was introduced as the solution. The power grid must maintain real-time balance between supply and demand, but electricity consumption varies significantly:
•	Day and night cycles create peak and off-peak periods
•	Weekends, holidays, and seasonal changes (summer vs. winter) cause demand fluctuations
•	Industrial and residential patterns differ substantially
Energy storage systems bridge the gap – storing excess electricity during low-demand periods and releasing it during peak hours, making the grid more reliable, economical, and efficient.
Functions and Applications of Energy Storage
The lecturer outlined the diverse functionalities of storage systems:
•	Peak shaving – reducing peak demand pressure
•	Frequency regulation – maintaining grid stability
•	Renewable integration – smoothing the output of solar and wind
•	Backup power – ensuring supply during outages
•	Mobile storage – used in electric vehicles, portable devices, and emergency response
Advanced Energy Storage Technologies
The lecture systematically introduced major storage technologies, their working principles, advantages, and limitations:

1. Lithium-Ion Batteries (Current Dominant Technology)
The lecturer showed a video demonstrating the working principle of lithium-ion batteries – lithium ions move between anode and cathode through electrolyte during charge/discharge cycles.
Advantages:
•	Fast response speed (milliseconds to seconds)
•	High energy density
•	Mature industry chain
•	Dominates over 96% of the new energy storage market 
Disadvantages:
•	Heat generation requires thermal management
•	Capacity degrades over time
•	Lithium resources are geographically concentrated and increasingly scarce
•	Recycling and disposal remain challenging
•	Safety concerns regarding thermal runaway

2. Sodium-Ion Batteries
Working Principle: Similar to lithium-ion but uses sodium ions instead – sodium shares similar chemical properties with lithium.
Advantages:
•	Sodium resources are abundant and widely distributed ("affordable resource") 
•	Low cost
•	Excellent performance in low temperatures (-30°C to 50°C) 
Applications: Suitable for high-altitude regions, grid peaking, and communication base stations.
Disadvantages: Lower energy density than lithium-ion; technology still maturing.

3. Flow Battery Energy Storage Systems
Working Principle: Unlike conventional batteries that store energy inside electrodes, flow batteries store energy in external liquid electrolytes contained in separate tanks. Electrolytes are pumped through the cell stack where redox reactions occur.
Advantages:
•	Very long cycle life (decades)
•	High safety (non-flammable electrolytes)
•	Independent scaling of power and capacity
•	Excellent for large-scale, long-duration storage
Disadvantages:
•	Low energy density
•	Complex system design
•	Higher initial cost
Real-world example: China has built and operates the world's largest vanadium flow battery storage project in Dalian, with Phase I reaching 100 MW / 400 MWh.

4. Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES)
Working Principle: Uses surplus electricity to compress air and store it in underground caverns, salt domes, or other large spaces. When electricity is needed, the compressed air is released to drive turbine generators.
Advantages:
•	Large storage capacity
•	No chemical reactions involved
•	Long service life (30–50 years)
•	Suitable for grid-scale, long-duration storage
Disadvantages:
•	Very high installation costs (requires geological formations or purpose-built containers)
•	Relatively low round-trip efficiency
•	Site-specific limitations
China's progress: Independently developed advanced CAES systems are continuously setting new single-unit power records.

5. Flywheel Energy Storage
Working Principle: Stores energy as rotational kinetic energy. A rotor (flywheel) spins at high speed (tens of thousands of RPM) in a vacuum chamber using magnetic bearings. Energy is drawn by slowing the rotor.
Advantages:
•	Extremely fast response (milliseconds)
•	Very high power density
•	Long cycle life
•	Environmentally friendly
Disadvantages:
•	Low energy density
•	High self-discharge rate
•	Expensive due to advanced materials and bearings
Applications: Primarily used for short-duration, high-power applications like frequency regulation, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), and grid stability services .

6. Thermal Energy Storage
Working Principle: Stores thermal energy by heating or cooling a storage medium for later use. Major types include:
•	Sensible heat storage – heating materials like water, rock, or concrete
•	Latent heat storage – using phase change materials (PCM) that store/release heat during melting/freezing
•	Thermochemical storage – using reversible chemical reactions
Key example – Molten Salt Thermal Storage:
Used in concentrated solar power (CSP) plants. Mirrors (heliostats) focus sunlight to heat molten salt, which retains thermal energy and can generate steam to drive turbines even after sunset.
Advantages:
•	Low cost for large-scale storage
•	High storage capacity
•	Long duration storage capability
Disadvantages:
•	Energy conversion losses (thermal to electrical)
•	Requires specialized materials and containment
•	Geographic constraints for certain applications

7. Hydrogen Energy Storage Systems
Working Principle: Excess electricity is used to split water via electrolysis, producing green hydrogen. The hydrogen can be stored and later used in:
•	Hydrogen fuel cells – converting hydrogen and oxygen back to electricity with zero carbon emissions
•	Hydrogen gas turbines – directly burning hydrogen for power generation
Advantages:
•	Zero carbon emissions (if green hydrogen)
•	Very long energy storage duration (weeks to months)
•	Can be transported and used in multiple sectors (power, transport, industry)
•	Hydrogen energy is elevated to national strategic status in China's energy policy
Disadvantages:
•	High construction and infrastructure costs
•	Low round-trip efficiency (electrolysis + fuel cell losses)
•	Storage and transportation challenges (hydrogen is highly diffusive and requires special materials)
•	Safety concerns
Future outlook: Hydrogen storage is considered a key technology for seasonal energy storage, helping balance renewable generation across months.

Technology Differentiation and Future Trends
The lecturer emphasized that different storage technologies serve different needs. Based on global development trends, a differentiated division of labor is emerging:
Time Scale	Dominant Technologies
Short-duration (< 0.5 hour)	Flywheels, supercapacitors, high-power lithium batteries 
Medium-duration (< 10 hours)	Lithium-ion batteries (evolving to solid-state), sodium-ion batteries 
Long-duration (> 10 hours)	Flow batteries, compressed air, hydrogen storage, molten salt thermal storage, iron-air batteries 
Future development directions include:
•	Solid-state batteries – using solid electrolytes to eliminate flammability, improve safety, and achieve higher energy density. Expected commercialization around 2028 .
•	Iron-air batteries – using reversible rusting to store energy for up to 100 hours .
•	AI-assisted materials discovery – machine learning accelerating battery material development and system optimization .

Summary and Reflections
The lecture on modern energy storage technologies provided students with a comprehensive understanding of why energy storage is essential for the renewable energy transition and how diverse technologies serve different roles. From lithium-ion's dominance to emerging solutions like sodium-ion, flow batteries, compressed air, flywheels, thermal storage, and hydrogen systems, the students learned that no single technology can solve all challenges – the future lies in a complementary, multi-technology ecosystem.
The lecturer also highlighted the urgent need for breakthroughs in safety, cost reduction, material sustainability, recycling, and manufacturing optimization  – challenges that present exciting opportunities for the next generation of energy engineers.

14:00 Session – Chinese Traditional Taijiquan Class
The afternoon session offered students a profound cultural and physical experience through the practice of Taijiquan (Tai Chi) , one of China's most treasured intangible cultural heritages. The class combined philosophical understanding, historical context, and hands-on practice, allowing students to embody the principles of balance, harmony, and mindfulness.
Opening Discussion: Chinese Naming System and Surnames
The teacher began with a lighthearted question – asking if everyone still remembered her name. This led to a brief explanation of the Chinese naming system, where the surname (family name) precedes the given name – the opposite of the order used in Uzbekistan and many other countries. The teacher asked if anyone could recall any common Chinese surnames. The students readily mentioned the surnames of their teachers – 张 (Zhāng), 李 (Lǐ), and 王 (Wáng) . The teacher then introduced several other popular Chinese surnames, noting that the "Hundred Family Surnames" (百家姓) historically listed over 500 family names still used in China today.
Introduction to Taijiquan – What is It?
Before delving into practice, the teacher showed several videos demonstrating the beauty and essence of Taijiquan, providing students with visual background and sparking their curiosity. She then asked if anyone had observed people practicing Taijiquan since their arrival in Jilin. The teacher noted that the most popular place to see this practice in Jilin City is Beishan Park, where locals gather in the early mornings to perform the flowing movements.
What is Taijiquan?
The teacher explained that "太极" (Taiji) means "Supreme Ultimate" – representing ultimate harmony, the oneness of opposites. Rooted in Daoist philosophy, Taiji is embodied through the dynamic interplay of Yin and Yang (阴阳) – the complementary forces that shape the universe.
Taijiquan is characterized by:
•	Slow, continuous, and circular movements (套路)
•	Coordinated breathing techniques
•	Focused mental attention and intent (意念)
Three Core Functions of Taijiquan:
1.	Health (健身): Improves flexibility, balance, cardiovascular health, and overall physical well-being.
2.	Meditation/Relaxation (放松/冥想): Reduces stress, promotes mindfulness, and calms the mind.
3.	Martial Art (自卫): Used for self-defense, emphasizing softness overcoming hardness – like water wearing down stone.
Taijiquan Schools
The teacher introduced two major schools of Taijiquan:
•	陈式太极拳 (Chen-style): The oldest and original form, characterized by a mix of slow and explosive movements, including jumps and stomps.
•	杨式太极拳 (Yang-style): Developed from Chen-style by Yang Luchan in the 19th century. It features slow, large, flowing movements and is more suitable for ordinary people to learn and practice due to its gentler, more accessible nature.
Philosophical and Cultural Roots
The teacher displayed the iconic Yin-Yang fish diagram (阴阳鱼图) , explaining that the S-curve represents the interdependence and complementarity of opposing forces – light and dark, activity and stillness, hardness and softness. The two fish in the diagram are always in motion, symbolizing the continuous, dynamic balance of the universe.
Origins: The founding father of Taijiquan is widely considered to be 陈王庭 (Chen Wangting) , a general during the late Ming Dynasty (around 1600 AD). He combined martial arts with traditional Chinese philosophical concepts and the theory of meridians from traditional Chinese medicine to create the "Art of Supreme Ultimate."
The teacher emphasized the deep connection between Taijiquan and Daoist philosophy:
•	Wu Wei (无为) – Action through inaction: Following the natural flow of energy, not forcing outcomes.
•	Overcoming hardness with softness (以柔克刚): Like water, which is soft yet can carve through stone over time.
•	Mindfulness and harmony: Developing mental and moral discipline – calmness, peacefulness, non-confrontation.
She also mentioned the concept of 天人合一 (Unity of Heaven and Humanity) – a state of perfect harmony between the individual and the universe.
Taijiquan and Chinese Culture
The teacher illustrated the cultural significance of Taijiquan with the example of the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games opening ceremony, where 2008 people performed a synchronized Taijiquan routine. The performance visually represented "Heaven around the Earth, Heaven and Humanity's Harmony" – demonstrating to the world the depth and beauty of this Chinese cultural treasure.
Practical Session – Learning Basic Taijiquan Movements
After establishing the philosophical and historical background, the teacher moved to the practical component. Students were taught five fundamental Taijiquan movements, each with specific hand positions, footwork, and breathing techniques:
Number	Chinese Name	Pinyin	English Translation
1	起势	Qǐ Shì	Beginning / Opening Form
2	野马分鬃	Yě Mǎ Fēn Zōng	Wild Horse Parting Its Mane
3	白鹤亮翅	Bái Hè Liàng Chì	White Crane Spreads Its Wings
4	搂膝拗步	Lōu Xī Ào Bù	Brush Knee and Push Step
5	手挥琵琶	Shǒu Huī Pí Pá	Play the Pipa (Chinese Lute)
The teacher emphasized that:
•	Breath must match movement – inhale on opening/rising, exhale on closing/sinking.
•	Movements must be soft and gentle – no force, no tension, only flowing grace.
•	Mind and body must be united – the movement flows from the core (dantian), not from isolated muscles.
Students practiced step by step under the teacher's guidance, with individual corrections for posture and technique. The teacher encouraged everyone to feel the internal energy (qi) and to move with calm, focused attention.
Presentation and Assessment
After sufficient practice time, each student was asked to come to the front of the class and demonstrate the five movements individually in front of everyone. Every student participated, showing visible progress from initial awkwardness to recognizable, flowing movements. The teacher provided gentle feedback, praising their efforts and encouraging continued practice.
Class Reflection
The Taijiquan class was much more than a physical activity – it was a profound cultural immersion. The students had the opportunity to:
•	Understand the philosophical depth behind Chinese martial arts.
•	Experience the mental and physical benefits of moving meditation.
•	Appreciate the Daoist principles of balance, harmony, and non-resistance.
•	Connect the practice to broader Chinese cultural values – health, spirituality, and moral cultivation.
Many students expressed feeling calmer and more centered after the practice – a direct experience of Taijiquan's meditative benefits. The class provided a perfect complement to the morning's technical lecture on energy storage, reminding students that balance and harmony apply not only to power grids and storage systems but also to the human mind and body.

Overall Summary for July 9, 2026
July 9 was a day of remarkable duality – combining technical rigor in the morning with cultural and physical wisdom in the afternoon:
•	The morning lecture on advanced energy storage technologies gave students a deep understanding of how the modern world manages electrical energy – from lithium-ion batteries and flow batteries to hydrogen storage and compressed air systems – addressing the challenges of renewable energy integration.
•	The afternoon Taijiquan class introduced students to the ancient Chinese philosophy of energy (qi) and its application through slow, controlled movement – a counterpoint to the high-tech world of power systems, yet connected by the same principles of balance, storage, and release.
Together, these sessions reinforced that energy – whether electrical or human – must be understood, stored, managed, and balanced with wisdom and harmony.
